questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four statements regarding the aerobic composting of sewage sludge.
  • Aim: Identify the TRUE statement(s) (Multiple Select Question).

2. Core Concepts & Solution Method:

Statement (A): Bulking agents and porosity
Sewage sludge has high moisture content and lacks sufficient voids. Bulking agents (wood chips, sawdust, rice husks) are added to increase porosity, allowing oxygen to permeate the pile and sustain aerobic microorganisms. The statement claims bulking agents reduce porosity — the exact opposite of their purpose. (FALSE)

Statement (B): Leachate generation
Due to the naturally high moisture content of sludge and the water released as a byproduct of organic breakdown:\[C_xH_yO_z + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O\]excess water percolates downward, creating leachate that must be collected and treated. (TRUE)

Statement (C): Actinomycetes involvement
The biological succession in aerobic composting involves mesophilic bacteria, thermophilic bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes. Actinomycetes thrive in the latter and thermophilic phases, breaking down complex organics (lignin, cellulose) and giving compost its characteristic earthy smell. (TRUE)

Statement (D): In-vessel composting modes
In-vessel composting systems (rotary drums, tunnel reactors, trench silos) are specifically designed as continuous plug-flow reactors, where fresh material goes in one end and finished compost comes out the other progressively. The statement claims they "cannot" be operated in plug-flow mode — contradicting standard industrial practice. (FALSE)

3. Final Answer:

Statements (B) and (C) are true | Option(s): B, C

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The theoretical aerobic oxidation of biomass (C₅H₇O₂N) is given below:
C₅H₇O₂N + 5O₂ → 5CO₂ + NH₃ + 2H₂O
The biochemical oxidation of biomass is assumed as a first-order reaction with a rate constant of 0.23/d at 20°C (logarithm to base e). Neglecting the second-stage oxygen demand from its biochemical oxidation, the ratio of BOD₅ at 20°C to total organic carbon (TOC) of biomass is _________________ (round off to two decimal places).
[Consider the atomic weights of C, H, O and N as 12 g/mol, 1 g/mol, 16 g/mol and 14 g/mol, respectively]
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Quality (BOD Kinetics)

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Biomass reaction: \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_7\text{O}_2\text{N} + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 5\text{CO}_2 + \text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
    • First-order BOD rate constant at 20°C: \(k = 0.23\text{ d}^{-1}\) (base \(e\))
    • Second-stage (nitrogenous) oxygen demand is neglected.
    • Atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14 g/mol
  • Aim: Find the ratio \(BOD_5 / TOC\) of the biomass.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Total Organic Carbon (TOC): Mass of elemental carbon present in a given molecule.
  • Ultimate Carbonaceous BOD (\(L_0\)): Theoretical oxygen demand for the carbonaceous stage only. From the balanced equation, 1 mole of biomass demands 5 moles of \(\text{O}_2\).
  • First-Order BOD Kinetics:\[BOD_t = L_0\left(1 - e^{-k\cdot t}\right)\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the mass of Carbon in 1 mole of biomass (TOC).
  2. Find the mass of \(\text{O}_2\) required for 1 mole of biomass (Ultimate CBOD, \(L_0\)).
  3. Apply BOD kinetics to find \(BOD_5\) over 5 days.
  4. Compute the ratio \(BOD_5 / TOC\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate TOC:\[\text{TOC} = 5 \times 12 = 60\text{ g/mol}\]
  2. Calculate Ultimate Carbonaceous BOD (\(L_0\)):
    From stoichiometry, 1 mole of biomass reacts with 5 moles of \(\text{O}_2\):\[L_0 = 5 \times 32 = 160\text{ g/mol}\]
  3. Calculate \(BOD_5\) at 20°C:\[BOD_5 = 160 \times \left(1 - e^{-0.23 \times 5}\right) = 160 \times \left(1 - e^{-1.15}\right)\]\[BOD_5 = 160 \times (1 - 0.316637) = 160 \times 0.683363 = 109.338\text{ g/mol}\]
  4. Calculate the Ratio:\[\dfrac{BOD_5}{\text{TOC}} = \dfrac{109.338}{60} = 1.8223 \approx 1.82\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{BOD_5}{TOC} = \mathbf{1.82}\) | Accepted key range: 1.80 to 2.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A system of seven river segments is shown in the schematic diagram. The Rᵢ's, Qᵢ's, and Cᵢ's (i = 1 to 7) are the river segments, their corresponding flow rates, and concentrations of a conservative pollutant, respectively. Assume complete mixing at the intersections, no additional water loss or gain in the system, and steady state condition. Given: Q₁ = 5 m³/s ; Q₂ = 15 m³/s ; Q₄ = 3 m³/s ; Q₆ = 8 m³/s ; C₁ = 8 kg/m³ ; C₂ = 12 kg/m³ ; C₆ = 10 kg/m³. What is the steady state concentration (in kg/m³, rounded off to two decimal place) of the pollutant in the river segment 7? _________________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality & River Mixing

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • \(Q_1 = 5\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_1 = 8\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • \(Q_2 = 15\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_2 = 12\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • \(Q_4 = 3\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) (diverted/extracted flow from \(R_3\))
    • \(Q_6 = 8\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_6 = 10\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • Conservative pollutant (no decay), complete mixing at junctions, steady state.
  • Aim: Find the steady-state concentration \(C_7\) in segment \(R_7\) (in kg/m³).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation (Flow Balance):\[\sum Q_{in} = \sum Q_{out}\]
  • Mass Balance Equation:\[\sum(Q_{in} \cdot C_{in}) = \sum(Q_{out} \cdot C_{out})\]
  • Flow Split Principle: When a uniformly mixed stream (\(R_3\)) splits into branches (\(R_4\) and \(R_5\)), the concentration is identical in each branch: \(C_4 = C_5 = C_3\).

3. Solution Method:

  1. Node 1 (\(R_1 + R_2 \rightarrow R_3\)): Flow and mass balance to find \(Q_3\) and \(C_3\).
  2. Node 2 (\(R_3 \rightarrow R_4 + R_5\)): Flow balance to find \(Q_5\); concentration unchanged by split.
  3. Node 3 (\(R_5 + R_6 \rightarrow R_7\)): Flow and mass balance to find \(Q_7\) and \(C_7\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Node 1: \(R_1 + R_2 \rightarrow R_3\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_3 = Q_1 + Q_2 = 5 + 15 = 20\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Mass Balance:\[20 \times C_3 = (5 \times 8) + (15 \times 12) = 40 + 180 = 220\text{ kg/s}\]\[C_3 = \dfrac{220}{20} = 11\text{ kg/m}^3\]
  2. Node 2: \(R_3 \rightarrow R_4 + R_5\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_5 = Q_3 - Q_4 = 20 - 3 = 17\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Concentration (split does not alter concentration):\[C_5 = C_4 = C_3 = 11\text{ kg/m}^3\]
  3. Node 3: \(R_5 + R_6 \rightarrow R_7\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_7 = Q_5 + Q_6 = 17 + 8 = 25\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Mass Balance:\[25 \times C_7 = (17 \times 11) + (8 \times 10) = 187 + 80 = 267\text{ kg/s}\]\[C_7 = \dfrac{267}{25} = 10.68\text{ kg/m}^3\]

5. Final Answer:

\(C_7 = \mathbf{10.68}\text{ kg/m}^3\) | Accepted key range: 10.58 to 10.78

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The total hardness in raw water is 500 milligram per liter as CaCO3. The total hardness of this raw water, expressed in milligram equivalent per liter, is

(Consider the atomic weights of Ca, C, and O as 40 g/mol, 12 g/mol, and 16 g/mol, respectively.)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Total Hardness \(= 500\) mg/L as \(\text{CaCO}_3\). Atomic weights: Ca \(= 40\), C \(= 12\), O \(= 16\).
  • Aim: Convert hardness to milligram equivalent per liter (meq/L).

Core Concepts:

  • Equivalent Weight: The mass of a substance that reacts with or replaces 1 mole of hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)).
  • Equivalent Weight of \(\text{CaCO}_3\):
    • Molecular Weight \(= 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\) g/mol
    • Valency for hardness (divalent cations \(\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}\)): \(n = 2\)
    • Equivalent Weight \(= \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\) g/eq \(= 50\) mg/meq
  • Conversion Formula: \[\text{Concentration (meq/L)} = \dfrac{\text{Concentration (mg/L)}}{\text{Equivalent Weight (mg/meq)}}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Molecular Weight:\[MW_{\text{CaCO}_3} = 40 + 12 + (16 \times 3) = 100 \text{ g/mol}\]
  2. Calculate Equivalent Weight:\[\text{Eq. Wt} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50 \text{ g/eq} = 50 \text{ mg/meq}\]
  3. Calculate Concentration in meq/L:\[\text{Hardness (meq/L)} = \dfrac{500 \text{ mg/L}}{50 \text{ mg/meq}} = 10 \text{ meq/L}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{10 \text{ meq/L}}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q26
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: For wastewater coming from a wood pulping industry, Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and 5-day Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5) were determined. For this wastewater, which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Parameters (COD & BOD)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Wastewater from a wood pulping industry; COD and BOD\(_5\) determined.
  • Aim: Identify the correct relationship between COD and BOD\(_5\).

Core Concepts:

ParameterDefinitionMeasurement
CODChemical Oxygen Demand — total oxidizable matter (biodegradable + non-biodegradable)Chemical oxidation (~2 hours)
BOD\(_5\)Biochemical Oxygen Demand — biodegradable organic matter onlyBiological oxidation (5 days at 20°C)

Key Relationship: \(\text{COD} \geq \text{BOD}_5\)

Reason: COD measures ALL oxidizable matter while BOD\(_5\) measures only the biodegradable fraction.

Common Pitfalls:

  • Assuming COD = BOD for all wastewaters.
  • Not considering non-biodegradable organic matter.
  • Confusing BOD\(_5\) with ultimate BOD (BOD\(_u\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Wood Pulping Wastewater: Contains lignin, cellulose, hemicellulose; significant non-biodegradable organic fraction; high COD due to chemically oxidizable compounds.
  2. Compare COD and BOD\(_5\):
    AspectCODBOD\(_5\)
    Oxidizable MatterCompletePartial (biodegradable only)
    Time Required2–3 hours5 days
    Value for Industrial WWHigherLower
  3. Evaluate Options:
    OptionStatementValidityReason
    (A)COD > BOD\(_5\)✓ CorrectNon-biodegradable fraction exists
    (B)COD ≠ BOD\(_5\)✓ CorrectValues are not equal
    (C)COD < BOD\(_5\)✗ WrongPhysically impossible
    (D)COD = BOD\(_5\)✗ WrongOnly for purely biodegradable waste

Final Answer:

\(\text{COD} > \text{BOD}_5\) and \(\text{COD} \neq \text{BOD}_5\) | Correct Options: (A), (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q27
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Which of the following process(es) can be used for conversion of salt water into fresh water?
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Desalination Processes

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Need to convert salt water to fresh water.
  • Aim: Identify suitable desalination processes.

Core Concepts:

ProcessMechanismSalt Removal Capability
MicrofiltrationPore size 0.1–10 μm✗ Removes particles, NOT dissolved salts
ElectrodialysisElectric field moves ions through selective membranes✓ Removes dissolved ions/salts
UltrafiltrationPore size 0.01–0.1 μm✗ Removes macromolecules, NOT dissolved salts
Reverse OsmosisPressure > osmotic pressure across semi-permeable membrane✓ Removes dissolved salts

Key Principle: Only processes that can remove dissolved ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻) can desalinate water.

Common Pitfalls:

  • Confusing particle filtration with salt removal.
  • Not understanding pore size vs. ion size relationship.
  • Assuming all membrane processes remove salts.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Salt Water Composition: Primary salts are NaCl, MgCl\(_2\), CaSO\(_4\). Ion sizes are ~0.1–0.2 nm — much smaller than MF/UF pores.
  2. Process Evaluation:
    ProcessPore / MechanismRemoves Dissolved Salts?Suitable for Desalination?
    Microfiltration0.1–10 μm poresNo✗
    ElectrodialysisIon-exchange membranes + Electric fieldYes✓
    Ultrafiltration0.01–0.1 μm poresNo✗
    Reverse Osmosis< 0.001 μm effective + PressureYes✓
  3. Selection:
    • Electrodialysis: Uses electric potential to move ions through selective membranes.
    • Reverse Osmosis: Uses pressure to force water through a semi-permeable membrane, retaining salts.

Final Answer:

Electrodialysis & Reverse Osmosis | Correct Options: (B), (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Henry's law constant for transferring O2 from air into water, at room temperature, is \(1.3 \dfrac{\text{mmol}}{\text{liter·atm}}\). Given that the partial pressure of O2 in the atmosphere is 0.21 atm, the concentration of dissolved oxygen (mg/liter) in water in equilibrium with the atmosphere at room temperature is

(Consider the molecular weight of O2 as 32 g/mol)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (Gas Transfer)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Henry's Law constant \(K_H = 1.3\) mmol/(liter·atm); Partial pressure of O\(_2\) in air \(p_{\text{O}_2} = 0.21\) atm; Molecular weight of O\(_2\), \(MW = 32\) g/mol.
  • Aim: Calculate the equilibrium concentration of dissolved oxygen in water in mg/L.

Core Concepts:

Henry's Law: At constant temperature, the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas in equilibrium with the liquid:

\[C = K_H \times p_g\]

Where \(C\) = concentration of dissolved gas, \(K_H\) = Henry's Law constant, \(p_g\) = partial pressure of the gas.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate dissolved concentration in moles:\[C_{\text{O}_2} = K_H \times p_{\text{O}_2} = 1.3 \dfrac{\text{mmol}}{\text{L}\cdot\text{atm}} \times 0.21 \text{ atm} = 0.273 \dfrac{\text{mmol}}{\text{L}}\]
  2. Unit conversion to mg/L:
    Since \(1 \text{ mol} = 32 \text{ g}\), we have \(1 \text{ mmol} = 32 \text{ mg}\):
    \[C_{\text{O}_2} = 0.273 \dfrac{\text{mmol}}{\text{L}} \times 32 \dfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{mmol}} = 8.736 \text{ mg/L}\]
    Rounding to one decimal place: \(8.7\) mg/L.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{C_{\text{O}_2} = 8.7 \text{ mg/L}}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
In a water sample, the concentrations of Ca2+, Mg2+ and HCO3- are 100 mg/L, 36 mg/L and 122 mg/L, respectively. The atomic masses of various elements are: Ca = 40, Mg = 24, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16.

The total hardness and the temporary hardness in the water sample (in mg/L as CaCO3) will be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (Hardness & Alkalinity)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \([\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 100\) mg/L; \([\text{Mg}^{2+}] = 36\) mg/L; \([\text{HCO}_3^-] = 122\) mg/L; Atomic masses: Ca = 40, Mg = 24, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16.
  • Aim: Determine Total Hardness (TH) and Temporary Hardness in mg/L as CaCO\(_3\).

Core Concepts:

  • Equivalent Weight (EW): \(EW = \dfrac{\text{Molecular Weight}}{\text{Valency}}\)
  • Concentration as CaCO\(_3\): \[\text{Equivalent Concentration} = \text{Concentration of ion} \times \dfrac{EW_{\text{CaCO}_3}}{EW_{\text{ion}}}\]
  • Total Hardness (TH): Sum of multivalent metallic cation equivalents (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺).
  • Temporary Hardness: Also known as Carbonate Hardness (CH). Equal to the minimum of TH and Alkalinity:\[\text{Temporary Hardness} = \min(\text{TH},\ \text{Alkalinity})\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Equivalent Weights:
    • \(EW_{\text{CaCO}_3} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{Ca}^{2+}} = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{Mg}^{2+}} = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{HCO}_3^-} = \dfrac{61}{1} = 61\) g/eq
  2. Calculate Total Hardness (TH) as CaCO\(_3\):\[TH = 100 \times \dfrac{50}{20} + 36 \times \dfrac{50}{12} = 250 + 150 = 400 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]
  3. Calculate Alkalinity as CaCO\(_3\):\[\text{Alkalinity} = 122 \times \dfrac{50}{61} = 2 \times 50 = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]
  4. Determine Temporary Hardness:\[\text{Temporary Hardness} = \min(400,\ 100) = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\text{Total Hardness} = 400 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3, \quad \text{Temporary Hardness} = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A wastewater sample contains two nitrogen species, namely ammonia and nitrate. Consider the atomic weight of N, H, and O as 14 g/mol, 1 g/mol, and 16 g/mol, respectively. In this wastewater, the concentration of ammonia is 34 mg NH₃/liter and that of nitrate is 6.2 mg NO₃⁻/liter. The total nitrogen concentration in this wastewater is ________ milligram nitrogen per liter. (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data: Aqueous NH\(_3\) = 34 mg/L; Aqueous NO\(_3^-\) = 6.2 mg/L; Atomic weights: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16 g/mol.
  • Aim: Find the Total Nitrogen (TN) concentration in mg N/L.

Core Concepts:

  • Total Nitrogen (TN): Mass sum of elemental nitrogen in all nitrogen-containing compounds in the sample.
  • Nitrogen Mass Fraction:\[\text{Fraction of N} = \dfrac{\text{Atomic weight of N in molecule}}{\text{Molecular weight of compound}}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Molecular Weights:\[MW_{\text{NH}_3} = 14 + (3 \times 1) = 17 \text{ g/mol}\]\[MW_{\text{NO}_3^-} = 14 + (3 \times 16) = 62 \text{ g/mol}\]
  2. Elemental Nitrogen from Ammonia:\[\text{N from NH}_3 = 34 \times \dfrac{14}{17} = 34 \times 0.8235 = 28.0 \text{ mg N/L}\]
  3. Elemental Nitrogen from Nitrate:\[\text{N from NO}_3^- = 6.2 \times \dfrac{14}{62} = 6.2 \times 0.2258 = 1.4 \text{ mg N/L}\]
  4. Total Nitrogen:\[TN = 28.0 + 1.4 = 29.4 \text{ mg N/L}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{TN = 29.4 \text{ mg N/L}}\] Accepted range: 29.0 to 30.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A 2 % sewage sample (in distilled water) was incubated for 3 days at 27 °C temperature. After incubation, a dissolved oxygen depletion of 10 mg/L was recorded. The biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) rate constant at 27 °C was found to be 0.23 day⁻¹ (at base e).

The ultimate BOD (in mg/L) of the sewage will be___________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Engineering / BOD Kinetics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Sewage sample concentration = 2%; incubation period \(t = 3\) days; temperature = 27°C; DO depletion = 10 mg/L; BOD rate constant \(k_{27} = 0.23\) day⁻¹ (base \(e\)).
  • Aim: Calculate the ultimate BOD (\(L_0\)) in mg/L.

Core Concepts:

  • Dilution Factor (DF): A 2% sewage sample means 2 parts sewage in 100 parts total.\[DF = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\]
  • BOD Calculation: \(BOD_t = \text{DO Depletion} \times DF\)
  • First-Order BOD Kinetics:\[BOD_t = L_0\left(1 - e^{-k \cdot t}\right)\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate 3-day BOD of raw sewage:\[BOD_3 = 10 \text{ mg/L} \times 50 = 500 \text{ mg/L}\]
  2. Calculate Ultimate BOD (\(L_0\)):\[500 = L_0\left(1 - e^{-0.23 \times 3}\right) = L_0\left(1 - e^{-0.69}\right)\]\[500 = L_0(1 - 0.5016) = L_0 \times 0.4984\]\[L_0 = \dfrac{500}{0.4984} \approx 1003 \text{ mg/L}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{L_0 \approx 1003 \text{ mg/L}}\] Accepted range: 1000 to 1005

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A water treatment plant has a sedimentation basin of depth 3 m, width 5 m, and length 40 m. The water inflow rate is 500 m³/h. The removal fraction of particles having a settling velocity of 1.0 m/h is ________. (round off to one decimal place)

(Consider the particle density as 2650 kg/m³ and liquid density as 991 kg/m³)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment / Sedimentation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Basin depth \(H = 3\) m; width \(B = 5\) m; length \(L = 40\) m; inflow \(Q = 500\) m³/h; settling velocity \(v_s = 1.0\) m/h. (Particle and liquid densities are distractors — \(v_s\) is already given.)
  • Aim: Calculate the removal fraction of the particles.

Core Concepts:

  • Surface Overflow Rate (SOR, \(V_0\)): The settling velocity of the design particle that is 100% removed. Depends only on plan area, not depth:\[V_0 = \dfrac{Q}{B \times L}\]
  • Removal Fraction (\(\eta\)): For an ideal rectangular basin:
    • If \(v_s \geq V_0\): \(\eta = 1\) (100% removal)
    • If \(v_s < V_0\): \(\eta = \dfrac{v_s}{V_0}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Surface Area:\[A_s = B \times L = 5 \times 40 = 200 \text{ m}^2\]
  2. Surface Overflow Rate:\[V_0 = \dfrac{500}{200} = 2.5 \text{ m/h}\]
  3. Removal Fraction:
    Since \(v_s = 1.0 \text{ m/h} < V_0 = 2.5 \text{ m/h}\):\[\eta = \dfrac{v_s}{V_0} = \dfrac{1.0}{2.5} = 0.4\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\eta = 0.4 \quad (40\% \text{ removal})}\] Accepted range: 0.38 to 0.42

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q22
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A process equipment emits 5 kg/h of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). If a hood placed over the process equipment captures 95% of the VOCs, then the fugitive emission in kg/h is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Total VOC emission rate = \(5 \text{ kg/h}\)
    • Hood Capture Efficiency = \(95\%\)
  • Aim: Calculate the Fugitive Emission in kg/h.

3. Core Concepts:

Fugitive Emissions: Emissions escaping the capture hood (not released through a stack or duct).

Mass Balance: \(\text{Total Emission} = \text{Captured Emission} + \text{Fugitive Emission}\)

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the fraction escaping the hood as \((100\% - \text{Capture Efficiency})\) and multiply by total emission rate.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Fugitive fraction:
    \[100\% - 95\% = 5\% = 0.05 \]
  2. Fugitive emission rate:
    \[\text{Fugitive Emission} = 5 \text{ kg/h} \times 0.05 = 0.25 \text{ kg/h} \]
    Verification: Captured = \(5 \times 0.95 = 4.75\) kg/h; Fugitive = \(5 - 4.75 = 0.25\) kg/h ✓

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.25 kg/h | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A 100 mg of HNO₃ (strong acid) is added to water, bringing the final volume to 1.0 liter. Consider the atomic weights of H, N, and O, as 1 g/mol, 14 g/mol, and 16 g/mol, respectively. The final pH of this water is
(Ignore the dissociation of water.)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (pH & Chemistry)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Mass of \(HNO_3\) added = \(100 \text{ mg} = 0.1 \text{ g}\)
    • Final volume of water = \(1.0 \text{ L}\)
    • Atomic weights: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16 g/mol
  • Aim: Calculate the final pH of the water.

3. Core Concepts:

Molar Mass: Sum of atomic weights of constituent elements.

Strong Acid Dissociation: Nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) dissociates completely: \(HNO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + NO_3^-\). Therefore, \([H^+] = [HNO_3]_{\text{initial}}\).

pH Calculation: \(pH = -\log_{10}[H^+]\)

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the molar mass of \(HNO_3\), convert the given mass to moles, find the molar concentration in 1.0 L, and apply the pH formula.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Molar Mass of \(HNO_3\):
    \[MW = 1 + 14 + (3 \times 16) = 1 + 14 + 48 = 63 \text{ g/mol} \]
  2. Moles of \(HNO_3\):
    \[n = \dfrac{0.1 \text{ g}}{63 \text{ g/mol}} = 1.5873 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol} \]
  3. Concentration of \(H^+\) ions:
    \[ [H^+] = \dfrac{1.5873 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0} = 1.5873 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M} \]
  4. Calculate pH:
    \[pH = -\log_{10}(1.5873 \times 10^{-3}) = 3 - \log_{10}(1.5873) = 3 - 0.2007 = 2.799 \approx 2.8 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.8 | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
In a city, the chemical formula of biodegradable fraction of municipal solid waste (MSW) is C₁₀₀H₂₅₀O₈₀N. The waste has to be treated by forced-aeration composting process for which air requirement has to be estimated.

Assume oxygen in air (by weight) = 23 %, and density of air = 1.3 kg/m³. Atomic mass: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14.

C and H are oxidized completely whereas N is converted only into NH₃ during oxidation.

For oxidative degradation of 1 tonne of the waste, the required theoretical volume of air (in m³/tonne) will be (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Formula of biodegradable MSW: \(C_{100}H_{250}O_{80}N\)
    • Oxygen in air by weight = \(23\%\)
    • Density of air, \(\rho_{air} = 1.3 \text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • Waste quantity = \(1 \text{ tonne} = 1000 \text{ kg}\)
    • Atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14
    • Oxidation rules: C → CO₂, H → H₂O, N → NH₃
  • Aim: Determine the theoretical volume of air required (in m³/tonne) for complete oxidative degradation.

3. Core Concepts:

Stoichiometry of Combustion: Balancing a chemical equation based on conservation of mass.

Mass Fraction: Total mass of air = mass of O₂ required ÷ oxygen mass fraction in air.

Volume-Density Relation: \(\text{Volume} = \text{Mass} / \text{Density}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Formulate and balance the chemical reaction for oxidation of MSW.
  2. Calculate MW of MSW and mass of O₂ required per unit mass.
  3. Scale up for 1 tonne of MSW.
  4. Convert required O₂ mass to air mass, then to air volume.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Balance the chemical equation:
    \[C_{100}H_{250}O_{80}N + x\,O_2 \rightarrow a\,CO_2 + b\,H_2O + c\,NH_3 \]
    • C balance: \(a = 100\)
    • N balance: \(c = 1\)
    • H balance: \(250 = 2b + 3(1) \Rightarrow b = 123.5\)
    • O balance: \(80 + 2x = 2(100) + 123.5 \Rightarrow x = 121.75\)
  2. Molecular Weights:
    \[MW_{\text{MSW}} = (100 \times 12) + (250 \times 1) + (80 \times 16) + (1 \times 14) = 2744 \text{ kg/kmol} \]
    \[MW_{O_2\,\text{required}} = 121.75 \times 32 = 3896 \text{ kg/kmol} \]
  3. Mass of O₂ for 1000 kg of MSW:
    \[m_{O_2} = \dfrac{3896}{2744} \times 1000 = 1419.825 \text{ kg} \]
  4. Mass and Volume of Air:
    \[m_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{1419.825}{0.23} = 6173.152 \text{ kg} \]
    \[V_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{6173.152}{1.3} = 4748.578 \text{ m}^3 \approx 4749 \text{ m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4749 m³/tonne | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The concentration s(x, t) of pollutants in a one-dimensional reservoir at position x and time t satisfies the diffusion equation
\[\dfrac{\partial s(x,t)}{\partial t} = D \dfrac{\partial^2 s(x,t)}{\partial x^2} \]
on the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ L, where D is the diffusion coefficient of the pollutants. The initial condition s(x, 0) is defined by the step-function shown in the figure.



The boundary conditions of the problem are given by \( \dfrac{\partial s(x,t)}{\partial x} = 0 \) at the boundary points x = 0 and x = L at all times. Consider D = 0.1 m²/s, s₀ = 5 µmol/m, and L = 10 m.

The steady-state concentration \( \hat{s}\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = s\left(\dfrac{L}{2}, \infty\right) \) at the center \( x = \dfrac{L}{2} \) of the reservoir (in µmol/m) is _________. (in integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Mass Transfer / Diffusion

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • 1D Diffusion equation: \(\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial t} = D \dfrac{\partial^2 s}{\partial x^2}\)
    • Domain length: \(L = 10 \text{ m}\)
    • Boundary Conditions: \(\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x} = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) (No-flux boundaries)
    • Diffusion Coefficient: \(D = 0.1 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}\)
    • Initial Condition: \(s = s_0\) for \(0 \le x \le 0.4L\), and \(s = 0\) for \(0.4L < x \le L\)
    • Initial concentration: \(s_0 = 5 \, \mu\text{mol/m}\)
  • Aim: Find the steady-state concentration \(\tilde{s}(L/2, \infty)\) in \(\mu\text{mol/m}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Conservation of Mass: The no-flux boundary conditions mean zero mass enters or leaves — the system is closed and total pollutant mass is conserved.

Steady-State Uniformity: At \(t \to \infty\), diffusion forces the concentration gradient to zero everywhere, resulting in a uniform distribution across the entire domain.

Note: The values of \(D\) and \(L\) dictate how fast steady state is reached, but are distractors for finding the final concentration value.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate total initial mass by integrating the initial concentration profile.
  2. Set final steady-state concentration as uniform constant \(\tilde{s}\).
  3. Equate initial and final mass (conservation) to solve for \(\tilde{s}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Initial Mass:
    \[M_{initial} = \int_0^L s(x,0)\,dx = s_0 \times 0.4L = 0.4\,s_0\,L \]
  2. Total Final Mass:
    \[M_{final} = \tilde{s} \cdot L \]
  3. Apply Conservation of Mass:
    \[0.4\,s_0\,L = \tilde{s}\,L \implies \tilde{s} = 0.4\,s_0 \]
  4. Substitute Values:
    \[\tilde{s} = 0.4 \times 5 = 2 \, \mu\text{mol/m} \]
    Since concentration is uniform at \(t = \infty\), the value at \(x = L/2\) is also \(2 \, \mu\text{mol/m}\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2 μmol/m | Accepted key range: 2 to 2

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: At a municipal waste handling facility, 30 metric ton mixture of food waste, yard waste, and paper waste was available. The moisture content of this mixture was found to be 10%. The ideal moisture content for composting this mixture is 50%. The amount of water to be added to this mixture to bring its moisture content to the ideal condition is _________ metric ton. (in integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial total mass, \(W_1 = 30 \text{ MT}\) (Metric Tons)
    • Initial moisture content, \(M_1 = 10\% = 0.10\)
    • Ideal (target) moisture content, \(M_2 = 50\% = 0.50\)
  • Aim: Amount of water to be added (\(W_w\)) in MT.

3. Core Concepts:

Mass Conservation: In a composting/drying process where only water is added or removed, the Dry Mass (\(W_d\)) remains constant.

Relationship between Total Mass, Dry Mass, and Moisture Content: \[W_d = W_{total} \times (1 - M) \] where \(M\) is the moisture content expressed as a decimal fraction.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the constant dry mass of the solid waste.
  2. Use the ideal final moisture content and the constant dry mass to find the new total mass (\(W_2\)).
  3. The amount of water added is the difference between the final total mass and the initial total mass.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Dry Solid Mass:
    \[W_d = 30 \times (1 - 0.10) = 30 \times 0.90 = 27 \text{ MT} \]
  2. Calculate Final Total Mass (\(W_2\)):
    Let the new total mass be \(W_2\). The moisture content is 50%, so the dry fraction is \((1 - 0.50) = 0.50\).
    \[W_d = W_2 \times (1 - 0.50) \implies 27 = W_2 \times 0.50 \implies W_2 = \dfrac{27}{0.50} = 54 \text{ MT} \]
  3. Calculate Added Water:
    \[W_w = W_2 - W_1 = 54 - 30 = 24 \text{ MT} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 24 | Accepted key range: 24 to 24

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A sewage treatment plant receives sewage at a flow rate of 5000 m³/day. The total suspended solids (TSS) concentration in the sewage at the inlet of primary clarifier is 200 mg/L. After the primary treatment, the TSS concentration in sewage is reduced by 60 %. The sludge from the primary clarifier contains 2 % solids concentration. Subsequently, the sludge is subjected to gravity thickening process to achieve a solids concentration of 6 %. Assume that the density of sludge, before and after thickening, is 1000 kg/m³.

The daily volume of the thickened sludge (in m³/day) will be_________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Sewage flow rate, \(Q = 5000 \text{ m}^3/\text{day}\)
    • Initial TSS concentration = \(200 \text{ mg/L}\)
    • TSS removal efficiency in primary clarifier = \(60\%\)
    • Initial sludge solids concentration = \(2\%\)
    • Thickened sludge solids concentration = \(6\%\)
    • Density of sludge (before & after thickening), \(\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Find the daily volume of the thickened sludge in m³/day.

3. Core Concepts:

Mass of Solids Extracted (\(M_s\)): \[M_s = Q \times \text{Initial TSS} \times \text{Removal Efficiency} \]

Mass-Volume Relationship for Sludge: \[V_{sludge} = \dfrac{M_s}{\rho_{sludge} \times \text{Solids Fraction}} \]

Note: The solid mass \(M_s\) remains constant during the gravity thickening process.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the daily mass of dry suspended solids removed by the primary clarifier. Use this constant solid mass, along with the given thickened sludge solids fraction and density, to determine the final sludge volume.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert Flow Rate to Liters/day:
    \[Q = 5000 \text{ m}^3/\text{day} = 5 \times 10^6 \text{ L/day} \]
  2. Calculate Mass of Removed TSS (\(M_s\)):
    \[\text{Removed TSS Concentration} = 200 \times 0.60 = 120 \text{ mg/L} \]
    \[M_s = (5 \times 10^6 \text{ L/day}) \times 120 \text{ mg/L} = 600 \times 10^6 \text{ mg/day} = 600 \text{ kg/day} \]
  3. Calculate Volume of Thickened Sludge:
    The thickened sludge has a \(6\%\) solid concentration (fraction = \(0.06\)).
    \[V_{thickened} = \dfrac{M_s}{\rho \times \text{Solids Fraction}} = \dfrac{600 \text{ kg/day}}{1000 \text{ kg/m}^3 \times 0.06} = \dfrac{600}{60} = 10 \text{ m}^3/\text{day} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 10 | Accepted key range: 10 to 10

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 2 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A sample of air analyzed at 25 °C and 1 atm pressure is reported to contain 0.04 ppm of SO₂. Atomic mass of S = 32, O = 16.

The equivalent SO₂ concentration (in µg/m³) will be ____________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Temperature, \(T = 25^\circ\text{C} = 298.15 \text{ K}\)
    • Pressure, \(P = 1 \text{ atm}\)
    • Volumetric concentration of SO₂, \(C_{ppm} = 0.04 \text{ ppm} = 0.04 \text{ mL/m}^3\)
    • Molecular Weight of SO₂, \(M = 32 + (2 \times 16) = 64 \text{ g/mol}\)
  • Aim: Equivalent SO₂ concentration in \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\).

3. Core Concepts:

Ideal Gas Law: Determines the volume occupied by one mole of gas (\(V_m\)) at given conditions. \[V_m = \dfrac{R T}{P} \] where Universal Gas Constant, \(R = 0.08205 \text{ L}\cdot\text{atm/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\)

Conversion Formula: \[C \,(\mu\text{g/m}^3) = \dfrac{C \,(\text{ppm}) \times M \,(\text{g/mol}) \times 10^3}{V_m \,(\text{L/mol})} \] (Since \(1 \text{ ppm} = 1 \text{ mL/m}^3\) and \(1 \text{ mole} = M \text{ g} = M \times 10^6 \, \mu\text{g}\).)

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the molar volume of an ideal gas at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) and \(1 \text{ atm}\). Then apply the standard conversion formula to shift from parts per million (volumetric) to \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\) (mass-based).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Molar Volume (\(V_m\)):
    \[V_m = \dfrac{0.08205 \times 298.15}{1} = 24.463 \text{ L/mol} \]
  2. Convert ppm to \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\):
    \[C \,(\mu\text{g/m}^3) = \dfrac{0.04 \times 64 \times 1000}{24.463} = \dfrac{2560}{24.463} = 104.647 \, \mu\text{g/m}^3 \]
    Rounding off to the nearest integer gives 105.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 105 | Accepted key range: 102 to 108

Pyrolysis is an exothermic process, which takes place in the absence of oxygen.
Combustion is an endothermic process, which takes place in the abundance of oxygen.
Combustion is an exothermic process, which takes place in the absence of oxygen.

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Pyrolysis is an endothermic process, which takes place in the absence of oxygen.

structuredOptions.label: B

structuredOptions.label: D

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four statements comparing pyrolysis and combustion based on heat flow and oxygen requirement.
  • Aim: Identify the correct statement regarding the physical chemistry of these waste treatment processes.

3. Core Concepts:

Pyrolysis: Thermal decomposition of organic material at elevated temperatures in an inert atmosphere (absence of oxygen). Requires external heat energy to break chemical bonds without oxidation → endothermic process.

Combustion: Burning of substances in the presence of oxygen. Rapid oxidation releases significant heat and light energy → exothermic process.

Common Pitfall: Do not confuse the ignition energy needed to start combustion with the overall thermodynamic nature of the reaction — combustion yields a net positive heat release.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): Pyrolysis is endothermic, occurs without oxygen. → Correct.
  • Option (B): Pyrolysis is exothermic. → Incorrect (requires heat input).
  • Option (C): Combustion is endothermic. → Incorrect (releases heat).
  • Option (D): Combustion takes place in the absence of oxygen. → Incorrect (requires oxygen).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Pyrolysis is an endothermic process which takes place in the absence of oxygen.  |  Correct option: (A)

2. Problem Analysis:

3. Core Concepts:

Oxygen Sag Curve: Minimum DO occurs downstream of discharge point P at the critical distance where deoxygenation rate exceeds reaeration — not immediately at point P.

Microbiology of ASP: Primary decomposers in Activated Sludge Process use organic carbon as their carbon source (heterotrophs) and derive energy from chemical oxidation of organics (chemotrophs) → chemoheterotrophs.

BOD Kinetics: \(BOD_5 / BOD_{ultimate} = (1 - e^{-k \times 5}) < 1\) always.

Lake Ecology: A young, nutrient-poor lake = oligotrophic; old, nutrient-rich lake = eutrophic.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): DO is lowest at critical point \(D_c\) further downstream, not at discharge point P. → Incorrect.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: The most important type of species involved in the degradation of organic matter in activated sludge process based wastewater treatment is chemoheterotrophs.  |  Correct option: (B)

  • Aim: Identify which pair represents exclusively liquid forms of particulate matter.

3. Core Concepts:

Air pollutants classified by physical state of particulates:

  • Liquid Particulates: Mist (condensation of vapor), Spray (atomization of liquid)
  • Solid Particulates: Dust (crushing/grinding), Smoke (incomplete combustion), Fumes (condensation of metallic vapors), Fly Ash (coal combustion residue)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

OptionPairPhysical StatesCorrect?
(A)Dust & MistSolid & LiquidNo
(B)Mist & SprayLiquid & LiquidYes
(C)Smoke & SpraySolid & LiquidNo
(D)Fly Ash & FumesSolid & SolidNo

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Mist and Spray  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 1 | CE Q28
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A 50 mL sample of industrial wastewater is taken into a silica crucible. The empty weight of the crucible is 54.352 g. The crucible with the sample is dried in a hot air oven at 104 °C till a constant weight of 55.129 g. Thereafter, the crucible with the dried sample is fired at 600 °C for 1 h in a muffle furnace, and the weight of the crucible along with residue is determined as 54.783 g. The concentration of total volatile solids is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Quality

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Sample volume (\(V\)) = \(50 \text{ mL}\) = \(0.050 \text{ L}\)
    • Weight of empty crucible (\(W_{\text{empty}}\)) = \(54.352 \text{ g}\)
    • Weight of crucible + sample dried at 104°C (\(W_{104}\)) = \(55.129 \text{ g}\)
    • Weight of crucible + residue fired at 600°C (\(W_{600}\)) = \(54.783 \text{ g}\)
  • Aim: Determine the concentration of Total Volatile Solids (TVS) in \(\text{mg/L}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Total Solids (TS): The residue left after drying a sample at 104°C. It includes both volatile (organic) and fixed (inorganic) solids.

Total Fixed Solids (TFS): The residue remaining after igniting the dried sample at 600°C in a muffle furnace.

Total Volatile Solids (TVS): The portion of Total Solids that volatilizes (burns off) at 600°C.\[W_{\text{TVS}} = W_{104} - W_{600} \]

Concentration: Mass of target constituent divided by the initial volume of the sample.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the mass of Total Volatile Solids in grams by subtracting the fired weight from the dried weight.
  2. Convert the mass from grams (g) to milligrams (mg).
  3. Convert the sample volume from milliliters (mL) to Liters (L).
  4. Divide the mass in mg by the volume in L to get the concentration in mg/L.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Calculate the mass of Volatile Solids.\[W_{\text{TVS}} = W_{104} - W_{600} = 55.129 \text{ g} - 54.783 \text{ g} = 0.346 \text{ g} \]
  2. Step 2: Convert mass to mg.\[\text{Mass} = 0.346 \text{ g} \times 1000 \text{ mg/g} = 346 \text{ mg} \]
  3. Step 3: Convert volume to L.\[V = 50 \text{ mL} = 50 \times 10^{-3} \text{ L} = 0.050 \text{ L} \]
  4. Step 4: Calculate Concentration.\[\text{Concentration of TVS} = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = \dfrac{346 \text{ mg}}{0.050 \text{ L}} = 6920 \text{ mg/L} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(6920 \text{ mg/L}\)  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 1 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A water sample is analyzed for coliform organisms by the multiple-tube fermentation method. The results of confirmed test are as follows:

Sample size (mL)Number of positive results out of 5 tubesNumber of negative results out of 5 tubes
0.0150
0.00132
0.000114

The most probable number (MPN) of coliform organisms for the above results is to be obtained using the following MPN Index.

MPN Index for Various Combinations of Positive Results when Five Tubes used per Dilution of 10.0 mL, 1.0 mL and 0.1 mL
Combination of positive tubesMPN Index per 100 mL
0 – 2 – 411
1 – 3 – 519
4 – 2 – 022
5 – 3 – 1110

The MPN of coliform organisms per 100 mL is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (Bacteriology)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Confirmed test results for 5 tubes each:
      • \(0.01\text{ mL}\) sample size: 5 positive
      • \(0.001\text{ mL}\) sample size: 3 positive
      • \(0.0001\text{ mL}\) sample size: 1 positive
    • Standard MPN index table provided for standard dilutions: \(10.0\text{ mL}\), \(1.0\text{ mL}\), and \(0.1\text{ mL}\).
  • Aim: Calculate the actual MPN of coliform organisms per \(100\text{ mL}\) for the given sample.

3. Core Concepts:

Most Probable Number (MPN): A statistical method to estimate the viable numbers of bacteria in a sample.

Standard Table Format: Standard MPN tables are universally referenced to test volumes of \(10\text{ mL}\), \(1\text{ mL}\), and \(0.1\text{ mL}\).

Dilution Factor Scaling: When tested sample volumes differ from the standard table volumes, the table value must be multiplied by a scaling/dilution factor:\[\text{Actual MPN} = (\text{MPN from standard table}) \times \dfrac{\text{Largest standard volume}}{\text{Largest tested volume}} \]\[\text{Scaling Factor} = \dfrac{10\text{ mL}}{\text{Largest volume used in test}} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify the combination of positive results.
  2. Look up the corresponding standard MPN index from the provided table.
  3. Determine the dilution scaling factor between the tested volumes and the standard table volumes.
  4. Multiply the standard MPN index by the scaling factor.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: The positive tube combination from the test is \(5 - 3 - 1\) (for \(0.01\), \(0.001\), \(0.0001\text{ mL}\) respectively).
  2. Step 2: From the given table, the MPN index for a \(5 - 3 - 1\) combination is \(110\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) (applicable if the volumes were \(10\), \(1\), \(0.1\text{ mL}\)).
  3. Step 3: Calculate the scaling factor.
    • Standard largest volume \(= 10\text{ mL}\)
    • Tested largest volume \(= 0.01\text{ mL}\)
    \[\text{Scaling Factor} = \dfrac{10}{0.01} = 1000 \]
  4. Step 4: Compute Actual MPN per \(100\text{ mL}\).\[\text{Actual MPN} = 110 \times 1000 = 110{,}000\text{ per }100\text{ mL} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(110{,}000\text{ per }100\text{ mL}\)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Ammonia nitrogen is present in a given wastewater sample as the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) and ammonia (NH₃). If pH is the only deciding factor for the proportion of these two constituents, which of the following is a correct statement?
options: At pH above 9.25, only NH₄⁺ will be present.
At pH below 9.25, NH₃ will be predominant.
At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ and NH will be found in equal measures.
At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ will be predominant.

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: At pH above 9.25, only NH₄⁺ will be present.
structuredOptions.html: At pH above 9.25, only NH₄⁺ will be present.

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: At pH below 9.25, NH₃ will be predominant.
structuredOptions.html: At pH below 9.25, NH₃ will be predominant.

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ and NH will be found in equal measures.
structuredOptions.html: At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ and NH will be found in equal measures.

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ will be predominant.
structuredOptions.html: At pH 7.0, NH₄⁺ will be predominant.

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics (Chemistry)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Ammonia nitrogen exists as \(NH_4^+\) (ammonium ion) and \(NH_3\) (free ammonia).
    • pH governs their proportion.
  • Aim: Identify the correct statement regarding their relative dominance at specific pH values.

3. Core Concepts:

Acid-Base Equilibrium: Ammonia in water undergoes the following reversible dissociation reaction:\[NH_4^+ \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + H^+ \]

Dissociation Constant (\(K_a\)): The equilibrium is described by \(K_a = \dfrac{[NH_3][H^+]}{[NH_4^+]}\). For the ammonium ion at standard temperature (\(25^\circ\text{C}\)), \(pK_a \approx 9.25\).

Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation:\[ pH = pK_a + \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{[NH_3]}{[NH_4^+]}\right) \]

  • If \(pH = pK_a = 9.25\), then \(\log\left(\dfrac{[NH_3]}{[NH_4^+]}\right) = 0 \implies [NH_3] = [NH_4^+]\).
  • If \(pH < 9.25\): excess \(H^+\) shifts equilibrium left, favoring \(NH_4^+\).
  • If \(pH > 9.25\): basic environment shifts equilibrium right, favoring \(NH_3\).

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each statement against the equilibrium rules and identify the correct one.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Option (A): "At pH above 9.25, only \(NH_4^+\) will be present." → Incorrect. \(NH_3\) predominates above \(pK_a\). Also, "only" is chemically inaccurate as equilibrium maintains trace amounts of both.
  • Option (B): "At pH below 9.25, \(NH_3\) will be predominant." → Incorrect. Below 9.25, \(NH_4^+\) predominates.
  • Option (C): "At pH 7.0, \(NH_4^+\) and \(NH_3\) will be found in equal measures." → Incorrect. Equal measures occur exactly at \(pH = pK_a \approx 9.25\).
  • Option (D): "At pH 7.0, \(NH_4^+\) will be predominant." → Correct. Since \(7.0 \ll 9.25\):\[ \dfrac{[NH_3]}{[NH_4^+]} = 10^{(7.0 - 9.25)} \approx 0.0056 \]Thus, \(NH_4^+\) heavily dominates (\(>99\%\)).

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A baghouse filter has to treat 12 m³/s of waste gas continuously. The baghouse is to be divided into 5 sections of equal cloth area such that one section can be shut down for cleaning and/or repairing, while the other 4 sections continue to operate. An air-to-cloth ratio of 6.0 m³/min-m² cloth will provide sufficient treatment to the gas. The individual bags are of 32 cm in diameter and 5 m in length. The total number of bags (in integer) required in the baghouse is ___________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution Control

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Total waste gas flow \(Q = 12\text{ m}^3\text{/s}\)
    • Baghouse structure: 5 equal sections (4 active, 1 offline for cleaning)
    • Air-to-cloth ratio \(V = 6.0\text{ m}^3/\text{min·m}^2 = 6.0\text{ m/min}\)
    • Bag dimensions: Diameter \(D = 32\text{ cm} = 0.32\text{ m}\), Length \(L = 5\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total number of bags required in the baghouse.

3. Core Concepts:

Filtration Area Required: Determined by the flow rate and allowable air-to-cloth ratio during the most demanding state (1 section offline).\[A_{active} = \dfrac{Q_{total}}{V} \]

Surface Area of One Bag (ends not counted in active cloth area):\[A_{bag} = \pi \cdot D \cdot L \]

Total Bags: Must be equally distributed among all 5 sections.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert total flow rate \(Q\) to m³/min.
  2. Calculate active cloth area required for 4 functioning sections.
  3. Determine cloth area required per section.
  4. Calculate total cloth area installed across all 5 sections.
  5. Find number of bags per section (rounding up) and multiply by 5.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Convert Flow Rate\[Q_{total} = 12\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \times 60\text{ s/min} = 720\text{ m}^3\text{/min} \]
  2. Step 2: Active Cloth Area Required\[A_{active} = \dfrac{720}{6.0} = 120\text{ m}^2 \](served by the 4 online sections)
  3. Step 3: Area Per Section and Total Installed Area\[A_{\text{per section}} = \dfrac{120}{4} = 30\text{ m}^2 \]\[A_{\text{total installed}} = 30 \times 5 = 150\text{ m}^2 \]
  4. Step 4: Surface Area of One Bag\[A_{bag} = \pi \times 0.32 \times 5 = 1.6\pi \approx 5.0265\text{ m}^2 \]
  5. Step 5: Number of Bags\[\text{Bags per section} = \dfrac{30}{5.0265} = 5.968 \rightarrow \text{round up to } 6 \]\[\text{Total bags} = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{ bags} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 30 bags  |  Accepted key range: 30 to 30

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A secondary clarifier handles a total flow of 9600 m³/d from the aeration tank of a conventional activated-sludge treatment system. The concentration of solids in the flow from the aeration tank is 3000 mg/L. The clarifier is required to thicken the solids to 12000 mg/L, and hence it is to be designed for a solid flux of \( 3.2 \dfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{h}} \). The surface area of the designed clarifier for thickening (in m², in integer) is ___________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment / Secondary Clarifier

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Total flow from aeration tank, \(Q = 9600\text{ m}^3\text{/d}\)
    • Concentration of solids (MLSS), \(X_0 = 3000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Target thickened solids concentration, \(X_u = 12000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Limiting solid flux, \(SF = 3.2\text{ kg/(m}^2\text{·h)}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the surface area (\(A\)) of the designed clarifier required for thickening in m².

3. Core Concepts:

Solid Mass Balance: The total mass of solids applied to the clarifier per day (\(M_s\)) is the product of incoming flow rate and incoming solids concentration.\[M_s = Q \times X_0 \]

Area Requirement:\[A = \dfrac{M_s}{SF} \]

Note: The target thickened concentration (\(X_u\)) is a distractor for the area calculation via solid flux method. It would be used if calculating the underflow rate \(Q_u = \dfrac{QX_0}{X_u}\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert flow and concentration into compatible mass flow units (kg/d).
  2. Convert limiting solid flux from kg/(m²·h) to kg/(m²·d).
  3. Divide total solids mass by the converted solid flux to obtain surface area.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Total Mass of Solids Applied (\(M_s\))\[X_0 = 3000\text{ mg/L} = 3000\text{ g/m}^3 = 3\text{ kg/m}^3 \]\[M_s = 9600\text{ m}^3\text{/d} \times 3\text{ kg/m}^3 = 28{,}800\text{ kg/d} \]
  2. Step 2: Convert Limiting Solid Flux to Daily Basis\[SF = 3.2\text{ kg/(m}^2\text{·h)} \times 24\text{ h/d} = 76.8\text{ kg/(m}^2\text{·d)} \]
  3. Step 3: Required Surface Area\[A = \dfrac{M_s}{SF} = \dfrac{28{,}800}{76.8} = 375\text{ m}^2 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 375 m²  |  Accepted key range: 375 to 375

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Determine the correctness or otherwise of the following Assertion [a] and the Reason [r].

Assertion [a]: One of the best ways to reduce the amount of solid wastes is to reduce the consumption of raw materials.

Reason [r]: Solid wastes are seldom generated when raw materials are converted to goods for consumption.
options: Both [a] and [r] are true and [r] is the correct reason for [a]
Both [a] and [r] are true but [r] is not the correct reason for [a]

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Both [a] and [r] are true and [r] is the correct reason for [a]
structuredOptions.html: Both [a] and [r] are true and [r] is the correct reason for [a]

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: Both [a] and [r] are true but [r] is not the correct reason for [a]
structuredOptions.html: Both [a] and [r] are true but [r] is not the correct reason for [a]

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management – Assertion-Reason

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Assertion [a]: Source reduction of raw materials is one of the best ways to reduce solid waste.
    • Reason [r]: Solid wastes are seldom generated when raw materials are converted to goods.
  • Aim: Evaluate the logical correctness of [a] and [r] independently and their causal relationship.

3. Core Concepts:

Waste Management Hierarchy: The most preferred approach is Source Reduction (Reduce), followed by Reuse, Recycle, Recovery, and Disposal.

Industrial Ecology: Manufacturing is never 100% efficient. By-products, scrap, packaging waste, and defective items invariably constitute industrial solid waste (e.g., slag in steel production, tailings in mining, scrap in machining).

4. Solution Method:

  • Evaluate [a]: Reducing raw material consumption reduces the volume entering the waste stream and minimizes production waste. → True.
  • Evaluate [r]: The claim that waste is "seldom generated" during manufacturing is completely false — industrial processes generate massive amounts of solid waste. → False.
