questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q15
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The hardness of a water sample is measured directly by titration with 0.01 M solution of ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) using eriochrome black T (EBT) as an indicator. The EBT reacts and forms complexes with divalent metallic cations present in the water. During titration, the EDTA replaces the EBT in the complex. When the replacement of EBT is complete at the end point of the titration, the colour of the solution changes from
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Parameters – EDTA Titration (Hardness)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Titration: Water sample vs. 0.01 M EDTA
    • Indicator: Eriochrome Black T (EBT)
    • Reaction: EDTA replaces EBT in divalent metallic cation complexes
  • Aim: Identify the color change at the titration endpoint.

3. Core Concepts:

Determination of Total Hardness (IS 3025 Part 21): Hardness is caused by divalent cations (\(Ca^{2+}\) and \(Mg^{2+}\)); quantified using the EDTA titrimetric method.

Indicator Chemistry (EBT at pH 10, ammonia buffer):

  • Free EBT: Blue color
  • Metal-EBT complex (before endpoint): Wine Red color

Titration Mechanism: EDTA (strong chelating agent) progressively extracts metallic cations from the unstable Metal-EBT complex, forming a stable Metal-EDTA complex. At the endpoint, all metal ions are captured by EDTA and EBT is fully released in its free form.

4. Solution Method:

StageColor
Before endpoint (Metal-EBT complex present)Wine Red
At endpoint (free EBT at pH 10)Blue

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Wine Red → Blue | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Read the statements given below.

(i) Value of the wind profile exponent for the ‘very unstable’ atmosphere is smaller than the wind profile exponent for the ‘neutral’ atmosphere.

(ii) Downwind concentration of air pollutants due to an elevated point source will be inversely proportional to the wind speed.

(iii)Value of the wind profile exponent for the ‘neutral’ atmosphere is smaller than the wind profile exponent for the ‘very unstable’ atmosphere.

(iv) Downwind concentration of air pollutants due to an elevated point source will be directly proportional to the wind speed.

Select the correct option.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Four theoretical statements regarding atmospheric meteorology and the Gaussian plume model.
  • Aim: Identify the correct option that accurately classifies the given statements as True or False.

3. Core Concepts:

Wind Profile Power Law: The variation of wind speed with height is given by \(u_z = u_1\left(z/z_1\right)^p\). The exponent \(p\) depends on atmospheric stability:

  • The more unstable the atmosphere, the smaller the exponent \(p\) (closer to 0.1).
  • As stability increases (neutral → stable), \(p\) increases (reaching up to 0.6).
  • Unstable \(p\) < Neutral \(p\) < Stable \(p\)

Gaussian Plume Model: The downwind concentration \(C(x,y,z)\) of a pollutant from an elevated point source is inversely proportional to wind speed \(u\):

\[C \propto \dfrac{1}{u} \]

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each statement individually:

StatementClaimVerdict
(i)Exponent \(p\) for 'very unstable' < 'neutral'True
(ii)Downwind concentration is inversely proportional to wind speedTrue
(iii)Exponent \(p\) for 'neutral' < 'very unstable'False (it is the other way around)
(iv)Downwind concentration is directly proportional to wind speedFalse

Evaluating the options:

  • (A) (i) is False and (iii) is True — Incorrect
  • (B) (i) is True and (iv) is True — Incorrect (iv is false)
  • (C) (ii) is False and (iii) is False — Incorrect (ii is true)
  • (D) (iii) is False and (iv) is False — Correct

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Option (D) correctly identifies that both statement (iii) and statement (iv) are factually incorrect.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: (iii) is False and (iv) is False | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A water filtration unit is made of uniform-size sand particles of 0.4 mm diameter with a shape factor of 0.84 and specific gravity of 2.55. The depth of the filter bed is 0.70 m and the porosity is 0.35. The filter bed is to be expanded to a porosity of 0.65 by hydraulic backwash. If the terminal settling velocity of sand particles during backwash is 4.5 cm/s, the required backwash velocity is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Filtration)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Sand particle diameter (\(d\)): \(0.4\text{ mm}\)
    • Shape factor (\(\phi\)): \(0.84\)
    • Specific gravity (\(G\)): \(2.55\)
    • Original depth of filter bed: \(0.70\text{ m}\) (Redundant for this calculation)
    • Original porosity (\(n\)): \(0.35\)
    • Expanded porosity (\(n_e\)): \(0.65\)
    • Terminal settling velocity (\(v_t\)): \(4.5\text{ cm/s} = 0.045\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Find the required backwash velocity (\(v_b\)) to achieve the expanded porosity.

3. Core Concepts:

Filter Bed Expansion: During backwashing, the filter bed expands and fluidizes. The relationship between the backwash velocity (\(v_b\)), the terminal settling velocity of the particles (\(v_t\)), and the expanded porosity (\(n_e\)) is given by the empirical Fair-Geyer equation:

\[n_e = \left(\dfrac{v_b}{v_t}\right)^{0.22} \]

The exponent 0.22 is a standard empirical coefficient for typical filter sands, yielding an expansion index \(z = 1/0.22 \approx 4.545\).

Alternative form:\[v_b = v_t \cdot (n_e)^{4.545} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Rearrange the Fair-Geyer equation to solve for \(v_b\).
  2. Substitute the given values of \(n_e = 0.65\) and \(v_t = 4.5\text{ cm/s}\).
  3. Calculate the backwash velocity and match units with the options.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Formulate the equation for \(v_b\):\[v_b = v_t \cdot (n_e)^{\dfrac{1}{0.22}} \]
  2. Substitute the values:\[v_b = 4.5\text{ cm/s} \times (0.65)^{4.5454} \]
  3. Calculate the expansion multiplier:\[(0.65)^{4.5454} \approx 0.1410 \]
  4. Compute \(v_b\):\[v_b = 4.5 \times 0.1410 = 0.6347\text{ cm/s} \]
  5. Convert to m/s:\[v_b = 0.6347 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s} = 6.347 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s} \approx 6.35 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(6.35 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
An activated sludge process (ASP) is designed for secondary treatment of 7500 m³/day of municipal wastewater. After primary clarifier, the ultimate BOD of the influent, which enters into ASP reactor is 200 mg/L. Treated effluent after secondary clarifier is required to have an ultimate BOD of 20 mg/L. Mix liquor volatile suspended solids (MLVSS) concentration in the reactor and the underflow is maintained as 3000 mg/L and 12000 mg/L, respectively. The hydraulic retention time and mean cell residence time are 0.2 day and 10 days, respectively. A representative flow diagram of the ASP is shown below.



The underflow volume (in m³/day, round off to one decimal place) of sludge wastage is ______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment / Activated Sludge Process

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flow rate: \(Q = 7500\text{ m}^3/\text{day}\)
    • Ultimate BOD of influent: \(S_0 = 200\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Ultimate BOD of effluent: \(S_e = 20\text{ mg/L}\)
    • MLVSS in reactor: \(X = 3000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • MLVSS in underflow: \(X_u = 12000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Hydraulic Retention Time: \(\theta = 0.2\text{ day}\)
    • Mean Cell Residence Time (Sludge Age): \(\theta_c = 10\text{ days}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the volume of underflow sludge wastage \(Q_w\) (in m³/day).

3. Core Concepts:

Hydraulic Retention Time (\(\theta\)):\[\theta = \dfrac{V}{Q} \]

Mean Cell Residence Time (\(\theta_c\)):\[\theta_c = \dfrac{V \cdot X}{Q_w \cdot X_u + (Q - Q_w) \cdot X_e} \]

Standard Assumption: Unless specified, suspended solids escaping in the treated effluent (\(X_e\)) is assumed to be zero.

Note: The BOD values \(S_0\) and \(S_e\) are distractor data — they are not needed for this SRT-based calculation.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the volume of the ASP reactor (\(V\)) using \(Q\) and \(\theta\).
  2. Use the SRT formula to isolate and solve for wastage discharge rate \(Q_w\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Volume of Aeration Tank (\(V\)):\[V = Q \times \theta = 7500 \times 0.2 = 1500\text{ m}^3 \]
  2. Underflow Wastage Rate (\(Q_w\)):
    Assuming \(X_e = 0\), the SRT equation simplifies to:\[\theta_c = \dfrac{V \cdot X}{Q_w \cdot X_u} \implies Q_w = \dfrac{V \cdot X}{\theta_c \cdot X_u} \]\[Q_w = \dfrac{1500 \times 3000}{10 \times 12000} = \dfrac{4{,}500{,}000}{120{,}000} = 37.5\text{ m}^3/\text{day} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 37.5 m³/day | Accepted key range: 37.0 to 38.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2021 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A grit chamber of rectangular cross-section is to be designed to remove particles with diameter of 0.25 mm and specific gravity of 2.70. The terminal settling velocity of the particles is estimated as 2.5 cm/s. The chamber is having a width of 0.50 m and has to carry a peak wastewater flow of 9720 m³/d giving the depth of flow as 0.75 m. If a flow-through velocity of 0.3 m/s has to be maintained using a proportional weir at the outlet end of the chamber, the minimum length of the chamber (in m, in integer) to remove 0.25 mm particles completely is ______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment / Grit Chamber

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis & Application
  • Given Data:
    • Particle diameter: \(d = 0.25\text{ mm}\)
    • Specific gravity of particle: \(G = 2.70\)
    • Terminal settling velocity: \(v_s = 2.5\text{ cm/s}\)
    • Width of chamber: \(B = 0.50\text{ m}\)
    • Peak wastewater flow: \(Q = 9720\text{ m}^3/\text{day}\)
    • Depth of flow: \(H = 0.75\text{ m}\)
    • Flow-through velocity: \(v_f = 0.3\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Determine the minimum length of the chamber (\(L\)) in integer meters to achieve 100% removal of the 0.25 mm particles.

3. Core Concepts:

Discrete Particle Settling (Type-1): For complete removal, the settling time (\(t_s\)) must equal the hydraulic detention time (\(t_d\)).

\[t_d = \dfrac{L}{v_f}, \quad t_s = \dfrac{H}{v_s} \]

Equating the two:\[L = \dfrac{H \cdot v_f}{v_s} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all velocities to SI units (m/s).
  2. Perform a sanity check on flow-through velocity using \(Q = A \cdot v_f\).
  3. Calculate required length \(L\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit Conversions & Sanity Check:
    \(v_s = 2.5\text{ cm/s} = 0.025\text{ m/s}\)
    \[Q = \dfrac{9720}{24 \times 3600} = 0.1125\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[A = B \times H = 0.50 \times 0.75 = 0.375\text{ m}^2 \]\[v_f = \dfrac{0.1125}{0.375} = 0.3\text{ m/s} \; ✓ \]
  2. Minimum Length Calculation:\[L = H \times \dfrac{v_f}{v_s} = 0.75 \times \dfrac{0.3}{0.025} = 0.75 \times 12 = 9\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 9 m | Accepted key range: 9 to 9

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
During chlorination process, aqueous (aq) chlorine reacts rapidly with water to form Cl⁻, HOCl, and H⁺ as shown below

\[\text{Cl}_2 \text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl} + \text{Cl}^- + \text{H}^+ \]

The most active disinfectant in the chlorination process from amongst the following, is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Disinfection)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Chemical reaction of chlorine in water:\[\mathrm{Cl_2(aq) + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HOCl + Cl^- + H^+} \]Species formed: \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), \(\mathrm{H^+}\)
  • Aim: Identify the most active disinfectant species.

3. Core Concepts:

When chlorine is added to water, it hydrolyzes to form Hypochlorous acid (\(\mathrm{HOCl}\)) and Hydrochloric acid. At higher pH, \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) further dissociates into \(\mathrm{H^+}\) and Hypochlorite ion (\(\mathrm{OCl^-}\)).

Disinfection Efficiency: \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) is electrically neutral and highly unstable, allowing it to penetrate the negatively charged cell walls of bacteria far more effectively than \(\mathrm{OCl^-}\). \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) is approximately 80 times more effective than \(\mathrm{OCl^-}\). Species \(\mathrm{H^+}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) have no significant disinfectant properties.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Among \(\mathrm{H^+}\), \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), the universally accepted active disinfecting agent is \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) (Hypochlorous acid).

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: HOCl | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: An amount of 35.67 mg HCl is added to distilled water and the total solution volume is made to one litre. The atomic weights of H and Cl are 1 and 35.5, respectively. Neglecting the dissociation of water, the pH of the solution, is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Parameters

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Mass of HCl added: \(m_{\text{HCl}} = 35.67\) mg
    • Volume of distilled water: \(V = 1\) L
    • Atomic weight of H = 1 g/mol, Cl = 35.5 g/mol
  • Aim: Calculate the pH of the resulting solution (neglecting water dissociation).

3. Core Concepts:

Molar Mass of HCl: \(M_{\text{HCl}} = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5\) g/mol

Molarity: \(C = \dfrac{m \text{ (g)}}{M \times V \text{ (L)}}\)

Strong Acid Dissociation: HCl dissociates completely → \([\mathrm{H^+}] = C\)

pH Formula: \(\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Molar Mass of HCl

\[M_{\text{HCl}} = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5 \text{ g/mol} \]

Step 2: Moles of HCl

\[m = 35.67 \text{ mg} = 35.67 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g} \]\[\text{Moles} = \dfrac{35.67 \times 10^{-3}}{36.5} = 0.97726 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol} \]

Step 3: Molar Concentration of \(\mathrm{H^+}\)

\[ [\mathrm{H^+}] = \dfrac{0.97726 \times 10^{-3}}{1} = 0.97726 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol/L} \]

Step 4: pH Calculation

\[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(0.97726 \times 10^{-3}) = 3 - \log_{10}(0.97726) = 3 - (-0.010) = \mathbf{3.01} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.01 | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A river has a flow of 1000 million litres per day (MLD), BOD₅ of 5 mg/litre and Dissolved Oxygen (DO) level of 8 mg/litre before receiving the wastewater discharge at a location. For the existing environmental conditions, the saturation DO level is 10 mg/litre in the river. Wastewater discharge of 100 MLD with the BOD₅ of 200 mg/litre and DO level of 2 mg/litre falls at that location. Assuming complete mixing of wastewater and river water, the immediate DO deficit (in mg/litre, round off to two decimal places), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterRiverWastewater
    Discharge (MLD)1000100
    DO (mg/L)82
    BOD₅ (mg/L)5200
    Saturation DO: \(DO_{sat} = 10\) mg/L
  • Aim: Determine the immediate DO deficit (\(D_0\)) of the mixed stream.

3. Core Concepts:

Flow-Weighted Mass Balance:\[C_{mix} = \dfrac{Q_r C_r + Q_w C_w}{Q_r + Q_w} \]

Immediate DO Deficit:\[D_0 = DO_{sat} - DO_{mix} \]

Note: BOD₅ values are extraneous data for computing the immediate deficit — they are used for deficit at a later time \(t\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Mixed Stream DO

\[DO_{mix} = \dfrac{(1000 \times 8) + (100 \times 2)}{1000 + 100} = \dfrac{8000 + 200}{1100} = \dfrac{8200}{1100} = 7.4545 \text{ mg/L} \]

Step 2: Immediate DO Deficit

\[D_0 = 10 - 7.4545 = 2.5455 \approx \mathbf{2.55 \text{ mg/L}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.55 mg/L | Accepted key range: 2.45 to 2.65

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A water supply scheme transports 10 MLD (Million Litres per Day) water through a 450 mm diameter pipeline for a distance of 2.5 km. A chlorine dose of 3.50 mg/litre is applied at the starting point of the pipeline to attain a certain level of disinfection at the downstream end. It is decided to increase the flow rate from 10 MLD to 13 MLD in the pipeline. Assume exponent for concentration, n = 0.86. With this increased flow, in order to attain the same level of disinfection, the chlorine dose (in mg/litre) to be applied at the starting point should be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Disinfection)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Initial discharge \(Q_1 = 10\) MLD
    • Initial chlorine dose \(C_1 = 3.50\) mg/L
    • Increased discharge \(Q_2 = 13\) MLD
    • Dilution exponent \(n = 0.86\)
    • Pipe diameter \(D = 450\) mm, Length \(L = 2.5\) km (Volume is constant)
  • Aim: Calculate the new chlorine dose \(C_2\) required to maintain the same level of disinfection efficiency at the higher flow rate.

3. Core Concepts:

Watson's Law (Chick-Watson Law): The effectiveness of a disinfectant relates concentration (\(C\)) and contact time (\(t\)) via:\[C^n \cdot t = \text{Constant} \]where \(n\) is the empirical coefficient of dilution.

Hydraulics of the Pipe: Contact time in the pipe is:\[t = \dfrac{\text{Volume } (V)}{\text{Flow Rate } (Q)} \]Since the physical pipe size (\(V\)) remains unchanged: \(t \propto \dfrac{1}{Q}\)

4. Solution Method:

Set up Watson's Law for both the initial and final states. Substitute \(V/Q\) for \(t\), cancel the constant volume, and solve algebraically for \(C_2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Equate Disinfection Efficiencies

\[C_1^n \cdot t_1 = C_2^n \cdot t_2 \]

Step 2: Express time in terms of Volume and Discharge

\[C_1^n \cdot \dfrac{V}{Q_1} = C_2^n \cdot \dfrac{V}{Q_2} \]Volume \(V\) cancels from both sides:\[\dfrac{C_1^n}{Q_1} = \dfrac{C_2^n}{Q_2} \]

Step 3: Solve for \(C_2\)

\[C_2^n = C_1^n \cdot \dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} \]\[C_2 = C_1 \cdot \left(\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{n}} \]

Step 4: Substitute Values and Calculate

\[C_2 = 3.50 \times \left(\dfrac{13}{10}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{0.86}} \]\[= 3.50 \times (1.3)^{1.16279} \]\[= 3.50 \times 1.3570 \]\[= \mathbf{4.75 \text{ mg/L}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.75 mg/L | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) of a primary settling tank (discrete settling) is 20000 litre/m² per day. Kinematic viscosity of water in the tank is 1.01×10⁻² cm²/s. Specific gravity of the settling particles is 2.64. Acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s². The minimum diameter (in μm, round off to one decimal place) of the particles that will be removed with 80% efficiency in the tank, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Sedimentation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Surface Overflow Rate (SOR): \(V_c = 20000\) L/m²/day
    • Kinematic viscosity: \(\nu = 1.01 \times 10^{-2}\) cm²/s \(= 1.01 \times 10^{-6}\) m²/s
    • Specific gravity: \(G = 2.64\)
    • Target efficiency: \(\eta = 80\%\)
  • Aim: Minimum diameter of particles removed with 80% efficiency (in μm).

3. Core Concepts:

Discrete Settling Efficiency: \(\eta = \dfrac{V_s}{V_c} \times 100\%\), where \(V_s\) is the actual settling velocity.

Stokes' Law (laminar flow, \(Re < 1\)):\[V_s = \dfrac{g\,(G-1)\,d^2}{18\,\nu} \]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Convert SOR to m/s

\[V_c = \dfrac{20000 \times 10^{-3}}{1 \times 86400} = 2.3148 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Minimum Settling Velocity for 80% Efficiency

\[V_s = 0.80 \times 2.3148 \times 10^{-4} = 1.8518 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s} \]

Step 3: Particle Diameter from Stokes' Law

\[1.8518 \times 10^{-4} = \dfrac{9.81 \times (2.64-1) \times d^2}{18 \times 1.01 \times 10^{-6}} \]\[d^2 = \dfrac{1.8518 \times 10^{-4} \times 1.818 \times 10^{-5}}{16.0884} = 2.092 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}^2 \]\[d = \sqrt{2.092 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.446 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} = \mathbf{14.5 \text{ μm}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 14.5 μm | Accepted key range: 14.0 to 15.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A gaseous chemical has a concentration of 41.6 μmol/m³ in air at 1 atm pressure and temperature 293 K. The universal gas constant R is 82.05×10⁻⁶ (m³ atm)/(mol K). Assuming that ideal gas law is valid, the concentration of the gaseous chemical (in ppm, round off to one decimal place), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Concentration = \(41.6\) μmol/m³
    • Pressure: \(P = 1\) atm
    • Temperature: \(T = 293\) K
    • Universal gas constant: \(R = 82.05 \times 10^{-6}\) m³·atm/(mol·K)
  • Aim: Find concentration in Parts Per Million (ppm).

3. Core Concepts:

Ideal Gas Law: \(PV = nRT\)

Volumetric PPM: For gaseous pollutants, 1 ppm = 1 μmol of pollutant per 1 mol of air.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Moles of Air per Cubic Meter

\[\dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{P}{RT} = \dfrac{1}{82.05 \times 10^{-6} \times 293} = \dfrac{1}{0.02404} = 41.597 \text{ mol/m}^3 \]

So 1 m³ of air contains 41.597 moles.

Step 2: Concentration in PPM

\[\text{ppm} = \dfrac{\text{moles of pollutant}}{\text{total moles of air}} = \dfrac{41.6 \text{ μmol}}{41.597 \text{ mol}} = 1.00007 \text{ μmol/mol} \approx \mathbf{1.0 \text{ ppm}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.0 ppm | Accepted key range: 0.9 to 1.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A stream with a flow rate of 5 m³/s is having an ultimate BOD of 30 mg/litre. A wastewater discharge of 0.20 m³/s having BOD₅ of 500 mg/litre joins the stream at a location and instantaneously gets mixed up completely. The cross-sectional area of the stream is 40 m² which remains constant. BOD exertion rate constant is 0.3 per day (logarithm base to e). The BOD (in mg/litre, round off to two decimal places) remaining at 3 km downstream from the mixing location, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Stream Deoxygenation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Stream: \(Q_s = 5\) m³/s, Ultimate BOD \(L_s = 30\) mg/L
    • Wastewater: \(Q_w = 0.20\) m³/s, 5-day BOD \(= 500\) mg/L
    • Stream cross-sectional area: \(A = 40\) m²
    • Target distance: \(D = 3\) km \(= 3000\) m
    • BOD rate constant: \(k = 0.3\) day⁻¹ (base e)
  • Aim: Ultimate BOD remaining (\(L_t\)) at 3 km downstream in mg/L.

3. Core Concepts:

First-Stage BOD Kinetics: \(BOD_t = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) \implies L_0 = \dfrac{BOD_t}{1 - e^{-kt}}\)

Mass Balance at Discharge: \(L_{mix} = \dfrac{Q_s L_s + Q_w L_w}{Q_s + Q_w}\)

Remaining Ultimate BOD: \(L_t = L_{mix} \cdot e^{-kt}\)

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Ultimate BOD of Wastewater (\(L_w\))

\[500 = L_w(1 - e^{-0.3 \times 5}) = L_w(1 - e^{-1.5}) = L_w \times 0.7769 \]\[L_w = \dfrac{500}{0.7769} = 643.61 \text{ mg/L} \]

Step 2: Mixed Stream Ultimate BOD (\(L_{mix}\))

\[L_{mix} = \dfrac{(5 \times 30) + (0.20 \times 643.61)}{5 + 0.20} = \dfrac{150 + 128.72}{5.20} = 53.60 \text{ mg/L} \]

Step 3: Travel Time to 3 km

\[v = \dfrac{Q_{mix}}{A} = \dfrac{5.20}{40} = 0.13 \text{ m/s} \]\[t_s = \dfrac{3000}{0.13} = 23076.9 \text{ s} \implies t = \dfrac{23076.9}{86400} = 0.2671 \text{ days} \]

Step 4: Ultimate BOD Remaining at 3 km

\[L_t = 53.60 \times e^{-0.3 \times 0.2671} = 53.60 \times e^{-0.08013} = 53.60 \times 0.9230 = \mathbf{49.47 \text{ mg/L}} \]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 49.47 mg/L | Accepted key range: 49.00 to 50.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The relationship between oxygen consumption and equivalent biodegradable organic removal (i.e., BOD) in a closed container with respect to time is shown in the figure



Assume that the rate of oxygen consumption is directly proportional to the amount of degradable organic matter and is expressed as \( \dfrac{dL_t}{dt} = -kL_t \), where, \( L_t \) (in mg/litre) is the oxygen equivalent of the organics remaining at time \( t \) and \( k \) (in d⁻¹) is the degradation rate constant. \( L_0 \) is the oxygen equivalent of organic matter at time, \( t = 0 \).

In the above context, the correct expression is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics (BOD)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • First-order kinetics: \(\dfrac{dL_t}{dt} = -kL_t\)
    • \(L_t\) = oxygen equivalent of organics remaining at time \(t\) (mg/L)
    • \(L_0\) = ultimate BOD at \(t = 0\) (mg/L)
    • \(k\) = degradation rate constant (d\(^{-1}\))
  • Aim: Identify the correct mathematical expression relating BOD variables.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Ultimate BOD (\(L_0\)): Total oxygen required to degrade all organic matter.
  • BOD Remaining (\(L_t\)): Oxygen demand of organic matter still unoxidized at time \(t\).
  • BOD Exerted (\(\text{BOD}_t\)): Oxygen consumed by microorganisms up to time \(t\).
  • Mass Balance: \(L_0 = \text{BOD}_t + L_t\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate the rate equation to find \(L_t\).
  2. Apply mass balance to find \(\text{BOD}_t\).
  3. Evaluate each option against these results.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Integrate to Find \(L_t\)

\[\int_{L_0}^{L_t} \dfrac{dL_t}{L_t} = -k\int_0^t dt \implies \ln\left(\dfrac{L_t}{L_0}\right) = -kt \implies L_t = L_0\,e^{-kt} \]

Step 2: Find \(\text{BOD}_t\) by Mass Balance

\[\text{BOD}_t = L_0 - L_t = L_0 - L_0\,e^{-kt} = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) \]

Step 3: Evaluate Options

OptionExpressionVerdict
(A)\(\text{BOD}_5 = L_5\)✗ — BOD\(_5\) is oxygen consumed; \(L_5\) is oxygen remaining
(B)\(\mathbf{\text{BOD}_t = L_0 - L_t}\)✓ — Correct mass balance
(C)\(L_0 = L_t\,e^{-kt}\)✗ — Should be \(L_0 = L_t\,e^{kt}\)
(D)\(L_t = L_0(1 - e^{-kt})\)✗ — This is \(\text{BOD}_t\), not \(L_t\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\text{BOD}_t = L_0 - L_t\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution Control

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Suspended particle sizes: \(d_1 = 50\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) (coarse) and \(d_2 = 2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) (fine).
  • Aim: Identify the most suitable sequence of pollution control devices.

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Two identically sized primary settling tanks receive water for Type-I settling (discrete particles in dilute suspension) under laminar flow conditions. The Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) maintained in the two tanks are 30 m³/m².d and 15 m³/m².d. The lowest diameters of the particles, which shall be settled out completely under SORs of 30 m³/m².d and 15 m³/m².d are designated as \( d_{30} \) and \( d_{15} \), respectively. The ratio, \( d_{30}/d_{15} \) (round off to two decimal places), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment | Sedimentation Theory

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Type-I Settling (discrete particles, laminar flow)
    • \(SOR_1 = 30\text{ m}^3\text{/m}^2\text{·d}\) → lowest complete settling diameter \(d_{30}\)
    • \(SOR_2 = 15\text{ m}^3\text{/m}^2\text{·d}\) → lowest complete settling diameter \(d_{15}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the ratio \(\dfrac{d_{30}}{d_{15}}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Ideal Settling Theory: A particle is 100% removed when its terminal settling velocity \(v_s \ge SOR\). For the minimum diameter completely settled: \(v_s = SOR\).

Stokes' Law (Laminar): \[v_s = \dfrac{g(G_s - 1)d^2}{18\nu} \implies v_s \propto d^2 \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

\[\dfrac{SOR_{30}}{SOR_{15}} = \left(\dfrac{d_{30}}{d_{15}}\right)^2 \implies \dfrac{30}{15} = \left(\dfrac{d_{30}}{d_{15}}\right)^2 \] \[\dfrac{d_{30}}{d_{15}} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.41 | Accepted key range: 1.40 to 1.42

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Alkalinity of water, in equivalent/litre (eq/litre), is given by

\[\{\text{HCO}_3^-\} + 2\{\text{CO}_3^{2-}\} + \{\text{OH}^-\} - \{\text{H}^+\} \]

Where, { } represents concentration in mol/litre. For a water sample, the concentrations of HCO3- = 2×10-3 mol/litre, CO32- = 3.04 ×10-4 mol/litre and the pH of water = 9.0. The atomic weights are: Ca = 40; C = 12; and O = 16. If the concentration of OH- and H+ are NEGLECTED, the alkalinity of the water sample (in mg/litre as CaCO3), is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Parameters

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Alkalinity formula: \(\text{Alk (eq/L)} = [\text{HCO}_3^-] + 2[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] + [\text{OH}^-] - [\text{H}^+]\)
    • \([\text{HCO}_3^-] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol/L}\)
    • \([\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = 3.04 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol/L}\)
    • \([\text{OH}^-]\) and \([\text{H}^+]\) are neglected.
    • Atomic weights: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16.
  • Aim: Calculate total alkalinity in \(\text{mg/L as CaCO}_3\).

3. Core Concepts:

Equivalents to mg/L as CaCO\(_3\) Conversion:

  • Molecular weight of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\text{ g/mol}\)
  • Valency of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = 2\)
  • Equivalent weight \(= 100/2 = 50\text{ g/eq} = 50{,}000\text{ mg/eq}\)
\[\text{Alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO}_3) = \text{Alkalinity (eq/L)} \times 50{,}000\text{ mg/eq} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Plug the molar concentrations into the given formula to find Alkalinity in eq/L.
  2. Multiply by the equivalent weight of \(\text{CaCO}_3\) in mg/eq.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Alkalinity in eq/L

\[\text{Alk (eq/L)} = (2 \times 10^{-3}) + 2 \times (3.04 \times 10^{-4}) \] \[= 0.002 + 0.000608 = 0.002608\text{ eq/L} \]

Step 2: Convert to mg/L as \(\text{CaCO}_3\)

\[\text{Alk (mg/L)} = 0.002608 \times 50{,}000 = 130.4\text{ mg/L} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 130.4 mg/L as CaCO\(_3\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The ion product of water (pKw) is 14. If a rain water sample has a pH of 5.6, the concentration of OH− in the sample (in 10−9 mol/litre, round off to one decimal place), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (pH and Alkalinity)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Ion product of water: \(pK_w = 14\)
    • pH of rain water sample: \(5.6\)
  • Aim: Compute the concentration of hydroxide ions \([OH^-]\) in \(10^{-9}\) mol/litre, rounded to one decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

Ion Product Equilibrium: \[ [H^+][OH^-] = K_w \implies pH + pOH = pK_w \]

Definition of pOH: \[ pOH = -\log_{10}[OH^-] \implies [OH^-] = 10^{-pOH}\text{ mol/litre} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Find pOH using \(pH + pOH = 14\).
  2. Calculate \([OH^-] = 10^{-pOH}\).
  3. Convert to \(C \times 10^{-9}\) mol/litre format.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate pOH

\[pOH = pK_w - pH = 14 - 5.6 = 8.4 \]

Step 2: Find \([OH^-]\)

\[ [OH^-] = 10^{-8.4}\text{ mol/litre} \]

Step 3: Convert to \(10^{-9}\) base

\[10^{-8.4} = 10^{0.6 - 9} = 10^{0.6} \times 10^{-9} \approx 3.981 \times 10^{-9}\text{ mol/litre} \]

Rounded to one decimal place: 4.0

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.0 (\(\times 10^{-9}\) mol/litre) | Accepted key range: 3.8 to 4.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A waste to energy plant burns dry solid waste of composition: Carbon = 35%, Oxygen = 26%, Hydrogen = 10%, Sulphur = 6%, Nitrogen = 3% and Inerts = 20%. Burning rate is 1000 tonnes/d. Oxygen in air by weight is 23%. Assume complete conversion of Carbon to CO2, Hydrogen to H2O, Sulphur to SO2 and Nitrogen to NO2.

Given Atomic weights: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32

The stoichiometric (theoretical) amount of air (in tonnes/d, round off to the nearest integer) required for complete burning of this waste, is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management (Incineration)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    ComponentCOHSNInerts
    % by weight3526106320
    • Burning rate: 1000 tonnes/day
    • O\(_2\) content in air by weight: 23%
    • Atomic weights: H=1, C=12, N=14, O=16, S=32
  • Aim: Calculate the stoichiometric mass of air required in tonnes/day, rounded to the nearest integer.

3. Core Concepts:

Balanced Combustion Reactions:

  • \(C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2\) → 12 kg C needs 32 kg \(O_2\)
  • \(2H + 0.5O_2 \rightarrow H_2O\) → 2 kg H needs 16 kg \(O_2\)
  • \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\) → 32 kg S needs 32 kg \(O_2\)
  • \(N + O_2 \rightarrow NO_2\) → 14 kg N needs 32 kg \(O_2\)

Net Oxygen Demand: \(\text{Net }O_2 = \text{Gross }O_2\text{ needed} - O_2\text{ present in waste}\)

Air Requirement: \(\text{Air} = \dfrac{\text{Net }O_2}{0.23}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use 100 kg of waste as basis.
  2. Calculate \(O_2\) needed per element using stoichiometry.
  3. Subtract inherent oxygen (26 kg) to get net \(O_2\).
  4. Scale to 1000 tonnes/day and divide by 0.23.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: \(O_2\) Required per 100 kg of Waste

ElementMass (kg)\(O_2\) ratio\(O_2\) required (kg)
Carbon3532/1293.333
Hydrogen1016/280.000
Sulphur632/326.000
Nitrogen332/146.857
Gross \(O_2\) Required186.190

Step 2: Net \(O_2\) Requirement

\[\text{Net }O_2 = 186.190 - 26.000 = 160.190\text{ kg per 100 kg waste} \]

Step 3: Scale to Daily Burning Rate

\[\text{Total Net }O_2 = 160.190 \times \dfrac{1000}{100} = 1601.90\text{ tonnes/day} \]

Step 4: Determine Air Required

\[\text{Air} = \dfrac{1601.90}{0.23} = 6964.78 \approx 6965\text{ tonnes/day} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 6965 tonnes/day | Accepted key range: 6963 to 6967

questions.title: GATE CE 2020 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A sample of water contains an organic compound C8H16O8 at a concentration of 10−3 mol/litre. Given that the atomic weight of C = 12 g/mol, H = 1 g/mol, and O = 16 g/mol, the theoretical oxygen demand of water (in g of O2 per litre, round off to two decimal places), is _________.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics (ThOD)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Organic compound: \(C_8H_{16}O_8\)
    • Molar concentration: \(10^{-3}\text{ mol/litre}\)
    • Atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16 g/mol
  • Aim: Calculate the Theoretical Oxygen Demand (ThOD) in g of \(O_2\) per litre, rounded to two decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Generalized Oxidation Equation: For compound \(C_xH_yO_z\): \[C_xH_yO_z + \left(x + \dfrac{y}{4} - \dfrac{z}{2}\right)O_2 \rightarrow x\,CO_2 + \dfrac{y}{2}\,H_2O \]

Molar mass of \(O_2 = 32\text{ g/mol}\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Extract subscripts \(x, y, z\) from the formula.
  2. Calculate moles of \(O_2\) per mole of compound.
  3. Multiply by concentration and molar mass of \(O_2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Moles of \(O_2\) per mole of \(C_8H_{16}O_8\)
\(x = 8,\; y = 16,\; z = 8\)

\[\text{Moles of }O_2 = x + \dfrac{y}{4} - \dfrac{z}{2} = 8 + \dfrac{16}{4} - \dfrac{8}{2} = 8 + 4 - 4 = 8\text{ mol} \]

Sanity check: \(C_8H_{16}O_8 + 8O_2 \rightarrow 8CO_2 + 8H_2O\). Oxygen balance: \(8 + 16 = 16 + 8\). ✓

Step 2: Moles of \(O_2\) needed per litre

\[8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol/L} \]

Step 3: Convert to mass (ThOD)

\[\text{ThOD} = 8 \times 10^{-3} \times 32 = 256 \times 10^{-3} = 0.256\text{ g/L} \approx 0.26\text{ g/L} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.26 g/L | Accepted key range: 0.24 to 0.27

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q18
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Which one of the following is a secondary pollutant?
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: A list of air pollutants: Ozone, Carbon Monoxide, Hydrocarbon, Volatile Organic Carbon (VOC)
  • Aim: Identify the secondary pollutant among the given options.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Primary Pollutants: Emitted directly from a source in their original form (e.g., CO, SO\(_2\), NO\(_x\), Hydrocarbons, VOCs, Particulate Matter).
  • Secondary Pollutants: Formed in the atmosphere through complex chemical/photochemical reactions among primary pollutants and atmospheric constituents (e.g., Ozone \(\text{O}_3\), PAN, Photochemical Smog).

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each option based on its atmospheric origin mechanism and select the one formed via atmospheric reactions rather than direct emission.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

PollutantOriginType
Carbon Monoxide (CO)Direct emission from incomplete combustionPrimary
HydrocarbonDirect emission from unburned fuels & biological processesPrimary
VOCDirect emission from solvents, industry, vehicular exhaustPrimary
Ozone (\(\text{O}_3\))Formed by photochemical reaction of NO\(_x\) + VOCs in sunlightSecondary

6. Final Answer:

Ozone (\(\text{O}_3\)) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A completely mixed dilute suspension of sand particles having diameters 0.25, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45 and 0.50 mm are filled in a transparent glass column of diameter 10 cm and height 2.50 m. The suspension is allowed to settle without any disturbance. It is observed that all particles of diameter 0.35 mm settle to the bottom of the column in 30 s. For the same period of 30 s, the percentage removal (round off to integer value) of particles of diameters 0.45 and 0.50 mm from the suspension is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Completely mixed dilute sand suspension with particle diameters: 0.25, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50 mm
    • Column diameter \(= 10\) cm, Settling depth \(H = 2.50\) m
    • 100% of 0.35 mm particles settle to the bottom in \(t = 30\) s
  • Aim: Determine percentage removal of 0.45 mm and 0.50 mm particles in 30 s.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Discrete Particle Settling (Type I): Settling velocity \(v_s\) strictly increases with particle diameter \(d\). Larger particles settle faster.
  • Critical Settling Velocity (\(v_c\)): \(v_c = H/t\). Any particle with \(v_s \ge v_c\) is 100% removed.
  • Removal Efficiency: All particles with diameter \(d > d_c\) are completely removed (100%) since their \(v_s > v_c\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Evaluate the critical settling condition given by the 0.35 mm particle.
  2. Compare target particle diameters (0.45 mm and 0.50 mm) to the critical diameter.
  3. Deduce removal efficiency directly from settling velocity characteristics.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Critical condition: 0.35 mm particles achieve 100% removal in 30 s:\[v_c = \dfrac{2.50\text{ m}}{30\text{ s}} \approx 0.0833\text{ m/s} \]
  2. \(d_{0.45} = 0.45\text{ mm} > 0.35\text{ mm} \implies v_{s(0.45)} > v_c\)
  3. \(d_{0.50} = 0.50\text{ mm} > 0.35\text{ mm} \implies v_{s(0.50)} > v_c\)
  4. Both particles travel distance \(H\) in less than 30 s \(\implies\) 100% removal at the 30 s mark.

6. Final Answer:

Removal of 0.45 mm and 0.50 mm particles \(= 100\%\) | Accepted key range: 100 to 100

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Sedimentation basin in a water treatment plant is designed for a flow rate of 0.2 \( m^3/s \). The basin is rectangular with a length of 32 m, width of 8 m, and depth of 4 m. Assume that the settling velocity of these particles is governed by the Stokes’ law. Given: density of the particles = 2.5 g/cm³; density of water = 1 g/cm³; dynamic viscosity of water = 0.01 g/(cm.s); gravitational acceleration = 980 cm/s². If the incoming water contains particles of diameter 25 μm (spherical and uniform), the removal efficiency of these particles is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flow rate \((Q) = 0.2\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    • Basin dimensions: \(L = 32\text{ m},\ W = 8\text{ m},\ D = 4\text{ m}\)
    • Particle density \((\rho_p) = 2.5\text{ g/cm}^3\)
    • Water density \((\rho_w) = 1\text{ g/cm}^3\)
    • Dynamic viscosity \((\mu) = 0.01\text{ g/(cm}\cdot\text{s)}\)
    • Gravity \((g) = 980\text{ cm/s}^2\)
    • Particle diameter \((d) = 25\ \mu\text{m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the removal efficiency of these particles.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\)): The critical settling velocity required for 100% removal.\[V_o = \dfrac{Q}{\text{Surface Area}} \]
  • Stokes' Law: Calculates the actual settling velocity (\(V_s\)) of discrete spherical particles in a laminar regime.\[V_s = \dfrac{g (\rho_p - \rho_w) d^2}{18\mu} \]
  • Removal Efficiency (\(\eta\)): \(\eta = \left( \dfrac{V_s}{V_o} \right) \times 100\%\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all units to standard SI units (kg, m, s) for strict unit discipline.
  2. Calculate the Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\)).
  3. Calculate the settling velocity (\(V_s\)) using Stokes' law.
  4. Calculate the efficiency ratio.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Unit Conversions

  • \(Q = 0.2\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
  • \(\rho_p = 2.5\text{ g/cm}^3 = 2500\text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • \(\rho_w = 1.0\text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • \(\mu = 0.01\text{ g/(cm}\cdot\text{s)} = 0.001\text{ kg/(m}\cdot\text{s)}\) (or Pa⋅s)
  • \(g = 980\text{ cm/s}^2 = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • \(d = 25\ \mu\text{m} = 25 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Surface Overflow Rate (\(V_o\))

\[A_s = L \times W = 32\text{ m} \times 8\text{ m} = 256\text{ m}^2 \]\[V_o = \dfrac{Q}{A_s} = \dfrac{0.2}{256} = 7.8125 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} \]

Step 3: Settling Velocity (\(V_s\))

\[V_s = \dfrac{9.8 \times (2500 - 1000) \times (25 \times 10^{-6})^2}{18 \times 0.001} \]\[V_s = \dfrac{9.8 \times 1500 \times 625 \times 10^{-12}}{0.018} = \dfrac{9.1875 \times 10^{-6}}{0.018} = 5.1042 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} \]

Step 4: Removal Efficiency (\(\eta\))

\[\eta = \dfrac{V_s}{V_o} \times 100\% = \dfrac{5.1042 \times 10^{-4}}{7.8125 \times 10^{-4}} \times 100\% = 65.33\% \]

6. Final Answer:

Removal Efficiency \(= 65.33\%\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A sample of air analysed at 0°C and 1 atm pressure is reported to contain 0.02 ppm (parts per million) of NO₂. Assume the gram molecular mass of NO₂ as 46 and its volume at 0°C and 1 atm pressure as 22.4 litres per mole. The equivalent NO₂ concentration (in microgram per cubic meter, round off to 2 decimal places) would be ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution Metrics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Concentration of \(\text{NO}_2 = 0.02\) ppm
    • Temperature \(= 0^\circ\text{C}\), Pressure \(= 1\) atm
    • Gram molecular mass of \(\text{NO}_2\) \((M) = 46\) g/mol
    • Volume of 1 mole of gas at given conditions \((V_m) = 22.4\) L/mol
  • Aim: Convert the concentration from ppm to \(\mu\text{g/m}^3\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Parts Per Million (ppm) by Volume: 1 ppm means 1 volume unit of pollutant per \(10^6\) volume units of air.
  • Conversion Formula (derived from the Ideal Gas Law):\[\text{Concentration } (\mu\text{g/m}^3) = \dfrac{\text{Concentration (ppm)} \times M \times 1000}{V_m} \]The multiplier of 1000 converts from mg/m\(^3\) to \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify standard conditions: The volume of 1 mole is directly given as 22.4 L/mol (Standard Temperature and Pressure).
  2. Plug the values into the mass-to-volume conversion formula.
  3. Round off to two decimal places.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Apply Conversion Formula

\[C\ (\mu\text{g/m}^3) = C\text{ (ppm)} \times \dfrac{\text{Molecular Weight}}{\text{Molar Volume}} \times 1000 \]\[C = 0.02 \times \dfrac{46}{22.4} \times 1000 \]

Step 2: Computation

\[C = 0.02 \times 2.05357 \times 1000 = 41.07\ \mu\text{g/m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

\(C = 41.07\ \mu\text{g/m}^3\) | Accepted key range: 41.00 to 41.10

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A 0.80 m deep bed of sand filter (length 4 m and width 3 m) is made of uniform particles (diameter = 0.40 mm, specific gravity = 2.65, shape factor = 0.85) with bed porosity of 0.4. The bed has to be backwashed at a flow rate of 3.60 m³/min. During backwashing, if the terminal settling velocity of sand particles is 0.05 m/s, the expanded bed depth (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Filtration)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Initial Depth \((D_0) = 0.80\) m
    • Filter Area \((A) = 4\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m} = 12\text{ m}^2\)
    • Initial Porosity \((n_0) = 0.4\)
    • Backwash Flow Rate \((Q) = 3.60\text{ m}^3/\text{min}\)
    • Terminal Settling Velocity \((V_t) = 0.05\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Find the expanded bed depth (\(D_e\)) during backwashing in meters.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Richardson-Zaki Equation: Relates the backwash (approach) velocity \((V_B)\), terminal settling velocity \((V_t)\), and the expanded porosity \((n_e)\).\[V_B = V_t \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]The exponent 4.5 is standard empirical practice in Environmental Engineering for mixed-regime backwash typical of sand filters.
  • Conservation of Solids: The total volume of solid grains remains constant before and during expansion.\[D_0(1 - n_0) = D_e(1 - n_e) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the backwash velocity \(V_B\) from the flow rate and area (ensure units are in m/s).
  2. Use the Richardson-Zaki equation to solve for the expanded porosity \(n_e\).
  3. Use the solid conservation principle to solve for the expanded bed depth \(D_e\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Calculate Backwash Velocity (\(V_B\))

\[Q = 3.60\text{ m}^3/\text{min} = \dfrac{3.60}{60}\text{ m}^3/\text{s} = 0.06\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[V_B = \dfrac{Q}{A} = \dfrac{0.06}{12} = 0.005\text{ m/s} \]

Step 2: Calculate Expanded Porosity (\(n_e\))

\[V_B = V_t \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]\[0.005 = 0.05 \cdot (n_e)^{4.5} \]\[(n_e)^{4.5} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.05} = 0.1 \]\[n_e = (0.1)^{\dfrac{1}{4.5}} = (0.1)^{0.2222} \approx 0.5995 \approx 0.60 \]

Step 3: Calculate Expanded Depth (\(D_e\))

\[ D_e = D_0 \left[\dfrac{1 - n_0}{1 - n_e} \right] = 0.80 \left[\dfrac{1 - 0.40}{1 - 0.5995} \right] = 0.80 \left[\dfrac{0.60}{0.4005} \right] = 1.198\text{ m} \approx 1.20\text{ m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Expanded Bed Depth \(D_e = 1.20\) m | Accepted key range: 1.15 to 1.25

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A wastewater is to be disinfected with 35 mg/L of chlorine to obtain 99% kill of micro-organisms. The number of micro-organisms remaining alive (Nₜ) at time t, is modelled by Nₜ = N₀e⁻ᵏᵗ, where N₀ is number of micro-organisms at t = 0, and k is the rate of kill. The wastewater flow rate is 36 m³/h, and k = 0.23 min⁻¹. If the depth and width of the chlorination tank are 1.5 m and 1.0 m, respectively, the length of the tank (in m, round off to 2 decimal places) is ________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Disinfection

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Chlorine dosage \(= 35\) mg/L (distractor since reaction rate \(k\) is given independently)
    • Target efficiency \(= 99\%\) kill
    • Chick's Law model: \(N_t = N_0\, e^{-kt}\)
    • Rate constant \((k) = 0.23\text{ min}^{-1}\)
    • Wastewater flow rate \((Q) = 36\text{ m}^3/\text{h}\)
    • Tank Depth \((D) = 1.5\) m, Width \((W) = 1.0\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the required length of the chlorination tank.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Chick's Law: Describes first-order kinetics for the disinfection (die-off) of microorganisms.\[\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right) = -kt \]where \(N_t/N_0\) is the fraction of microorganisms surviving.
  • Hydraulic Retention Time (\(t\)):\[t = \dfrac{\text{Volume }(V)}{\text{Flow Rate }(Q)} \]
  • Tank Volume: \(V = L \times W \times D\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert the 99% kill requirement into the survival fraction (\(N_t/N_0\)).
  2. Use Chick's law to solve for the required contact time (\(t\)).
  3. Calculate the required tank volume by multiplying flow rate by contact time (ensuring matching time units).
  4. Solve for the unknown tank length (\(L\)) using the volume and given cross-sectional dimensions.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Step 1: Find Contact Time (\(t\))

99% kill means 1% survive: \(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0} = 1 - 0.99 = 0.01\)

\[0.01 = e^{-0.23t} \]

Taking natural log on both sides:

\[\ln(0.01) = -0.23t \implies -4.60517 = -0.23t \]\[t = \dfrac{4.60517}{0.23} = 20.0225\text{ min} \]

Step 2: Calculate Required Volume (\(V\))

\[Q = \dfrac{36\text{ m}^3/\text{h}}{60\text{ min/h}} = 0.6\text{ m}^3/\text{min} \]\[V = Q \times t = 0.6\text{ m}^3/\text{min} \times 20.0225\text{ min} = 12.0135\text{ m}^3 \]

Step 3: Calculate Tank Length (\(L\))

\[V = L \times W \times D \]\[12.0135 = L \times 1.0\text{ m} \times 1.5\text{ m} \]\[L = \dfrac{12.0135}{1.5} = 8.009\text{ m} \approx 8.01\text{ m} \]

Note: Chlorine dosage is extraneous information here, as the rate constant \(k\) is given directly and independently.

6. Final Answer:

Tank Length \(L = 8.01\) m | Accepted key range: 7.95 to 8.15

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q9
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Which one of the following options contains ONLY primary air pollutants?
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Four pairs of chemical air pollutants.
  • Aim: Identify the option containing ONLY primary air pollutants.

3. Core Concepts:

Primary Pollutants: Emitted directly into the atmosphere from a discernible source (e.g., vehicles, smokestacks, volcanic eruptions).
Examples: Carbon Monoxide (CO), Oxides of Nitrogen (NO\(_x\)), Sulfur Dioxide (SO\(_2\)), Hydrocarbons (HC) / Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), Particulate Matter (PM).

Secondary Pollutants: Not emitted directly. They form in the atmosphere when primary pollutants react chemically, often triggered by sunlight (photochemical smog).
Examples: Ozone (O\(_3\)), Peroxyacetyl Nitrate (PAN), Sulfuric Acid (H\(_2\)SO\(_4\)).

4. Solution Method:

Evaluate each pair in the given options to see if both elements belong to the "Primary Pollutant" category.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Option (A):
    • Hydrocarbons: Directly emitted from unburned fuel/exhaust → Primary
    • Nitrogen oxides: Directly emitted from high-temperature combustion → Primary
    • Status: Both Primary. ✓ Candidate for correct answer.
  2. Option (B):
    • Hydrocarbons: Primary
    • Ozone: Formed by reaction of NO\(_x\) and VOCs in sunlight → Secondary
    • Status: Mixed. ✗
  3. Option (C):
    • Ozone: Secondary
    • Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN): Formed in photochemical smog → Secondary
    • Status: Both Secondary. ✗
  4. Option (D):
    • Nitrogen oxides: Primary
    • Peroxyacetyl nitrate: Secondary
    • Status: Mixed. ✗

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q10
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Analysis of a water sample revealed that the sample contains the following species.
\(CO_3^{2-}, Na^+, H^+, PO_4^{3-}, Al^{3+}, H_2CO_3, Cl^-, Ca^{2+}, Mg^{2+}, HCO_3^-, Fe^{2+}, OH^-\)
Concentrations of which of the species will be required to compute alkalinity?
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: A water sample contains \(CO_3^{2-}\), \(Na^+\), \(H^+\), \(PO_4^{3-}\), \(Al^{3+}\), \(H_2CO_3\), \(Cl^-\), \(Ca^{2+}\), \(Mg^{2+}\), \(HCO_3^-\), \(Fe^{2+}\), \(OH^-\).
  • Aim: Identify which species' concentrations are required to compute the total alkalinity of the water sample.

3. Core Concepts:

Alkalinity: Alkalinity is the measure of the capacity of water to neutralize acids.

Major Contributors: In natural and treated waters, alkalinity is primarily imparted by the salts of weak acids (bicarbonates and carbonates) and strong bases (hydroxides).

Equation: The total alkalinity (in equivalent units) is theoretically calculated using the charge balance of the species that consume or donate protons:

\[ \text{Total Alkalinity} = [HCO_3^-] + 2[CO_3^{2-}] + [OH^-] - [H^+] \]

4. Solution Method:

From the fundamental equation of alkalinity, the buffering capacity primarily relies on Bicarbonate (\(HCO_3^-\)), Carbonate (\(CO_3^{2-}\)), Hydroxyl ions (\(OH^-\)), and it is opposed by the presence of Hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)). Although trace amounts of phosphates (\(PO_4^{3-}\)) or silicates can technically contribute, standard environmental engineering computations exclusively consider the carbonate system and water dissociation products unless otherwise specified.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify proton-accepting (alkalinity-contributing) species in the given list: \(CO_3^{2-}\), \(HCO_3^-\), and \(OH^-\).
  2. Identify proton-donating (alkalinity-reducing) species: \(H^+\).
  3. Species explicitly required for the calculation: \(CO_3^{2-}\), \(H^+\), \(HCO_3^-\), \(OH^-\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(CO_3^{2-}\), \(H^+\), \(HCO_3^-\), \(OH^-\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Chlorine is used as the disinfectant in a municipal water treatment plant. It achieves 50 percent of disinfection efficiency measured in terms of killing the indicator microorganisms (E-Coli) in 3 minutes. The minimum time required to achieve 99 percent disinfection efficiency would be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Disinfection)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Disinfection efficiency \(\eta_1 = 50\% = 0.5\)
    • Time \(t_1 = 3\) minutes
  • Aim: Find the minimum time (\(t_2\)) required to achieve \(\eta_2 = 99\%\) efficiency.

3. Core Concepts:

Chick's Law: The rate of destruction of microorganisms is directly proportional to the number of living microorganisms remaining.

\[N_t = N_0 \cdot e^{-kt} \]
  • \(N_0\) = Initial number of organisms
  • \(N_t\) = Surviving organisms at time \(t\)
  • \(k\) = disinfection rate constant

Efficiency (\(\eta\)):

\[\eta = \dfrac{N_0 - N_t}{N_0} = 1 - \dfrac{N_t}{N_0} = 1 - e^{-kt} \]

4. Solution Method & Execution:

  1. Step 1: Find the rate constant (\(k\)) using the 50% efficiency condition.\[0.5 = 1 - e^{-k(3)} \implies e^{-3k} = 0.5 \]Taking natural log on both sides:\[-3k = \ln(0.5) \implies k = \dfrac{0.6931}{3} = 0.231 \text{ min}^{-1} \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate the time (\(t_2\)) for 99% efficiency.\[0.99 = 1 - e^{-0.231 \cdot t_2} \implies e^{-0.231 \cdot t_2} = 0.01 \]Taking natural log on both sides:\[-0.231 \cdot t_2 = \ln(0.01) = -4.605 \]\[t_2 = \dfrac{4.605}{0.231} = 19.93 \text{ minutes} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 19.93 minutes | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A water treatment plant treats 6000 m³ of water per day. As a part of the treatment process, discrete particles are required to be settled in a clarifier. A column test indicates that an overflow rate of 1.5 m per hour would produce the desired removal of particles through settling in the clarifier having a depth of 3.0 m. The volume of the required clarifier, (in m³, round off to 1 decimal place) would be ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Plant flow rate: \(Q = 6000\) m³/day
    • Surface Overflow Rate (SOR): \(v_o = 1.5\) m/hour
    • Clarifier depth: \(H = 3.0\) m
  • Aim: Compute the required total volume of the clarifier.

3. Core Concepts:

Clarifier Surface Area: Governed purely by flow and overflow rate:

\[A = \dfrac{Q}{v_o} \]

Volume:

\[V = A \times H \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Standardize units: Convert daily flow rate \(Q\) into an hourly rate so it aligns with \(v_o\).
  2. Compute the required plan area \(A\).
  3. Multiply \(A\) by the required depth \(H\) to find the volume.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flow rate conversion:\[Q = \dfrac{6000\text{ m}^3/\text{day}}{24\text{ hours/day}} = 250\text{ m}^3/\text{hour} \]
  2. Calculate Plan Area (\(A\)):\[A = \dfrac{Q}{v_o} = \dfrac{250\text{ m}^3/\text{hour}}{1.5\text{ m/hour}} = 166.667\text{ m}^2 \]
  3. Calculate Volume (\(V\)):\[V = A \times H = 166.667\text{ m}^2 \times 3.0\text{ m} = 500.0\text{ m}^3 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 500.0 m³ | Accepted key range: 495.0 to 505.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Raw municipal solid waste (MSW) collected from a city contains 70% decomposable material that can be converted to methane. The water content of the decomposable material is 35%. An elemental analysis of the decomposable material yields the following mass percent.
C : H : O : N : other = 44 : 6 : 43 : 0.8 : 6.2

The methane production of the decomposable material is governed by the following stoichiometric relation
CₐHO꜀Nₔ + nH₂O → mCH₄ + sCO₂ + dNH₃

Given atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14. The mass of methane produced (in grams, round off to 1 decimal place) per kg of raw MSW will be ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Raw MSW mass base: 1 kg (1000 g)
    • Decomposable fraction: 70%
    • Moisture content in decomposable fraction: 35%
    • Elemental composition (on dry mass basis): C = 44%, H = 6%, O = 43%, N = 0.8%, Ash/Other = 6.2%
    • Reaction: \(C_a H_b O_c N_d + nH_2O \rightarrow mCH_4 + sCO_2 + dNH_3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the mass of methane (\(CH_4\)) produced (in grams) per 1 kg of raw MSW.

3. Core Concepts:

Moisture Content Adjustment: Elemental percentages are strictly given for the dry mass of solid waste.

Stoichiometry of Anaerobic Digestion: Balancing the carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen dictates the theoretical maximum methane yield. General stoichiometric formula:

\[m = \dfrac{4a + b - 2c - 3d}{8} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the actual dry mass of decomposable material available in 1 kg of raw MSW.
  2. Formulate the mole proportions for a 100 g chunk of the dry material to find coefficients \(a, b, c, d\).
  3. Substitute moles into the digestion stoichiometric equation to find the moles of \(CH_4\) produced.
  4. Scale up the \(CH_4\) mass yield from the 100 g sample to the full dry decomposable mass.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Mass Extraction:
    • Raw MSW \(= 1000\) g
    • Wet Decomposable Material \(= 0.70 \times 1000 = 700\) g
    • Dry Decomposable Material \(= 700 \times (1 - 0.35) = 455\) g
  2. Mole Coefficients (\(a, b, c, d\)) per 100 g dry material:
    • \(a\) (Carbon) \(= \dfrac{44}{12} = 3.6667\) mol
    • \(b\) (Hydrogen) \(= \dfrac{6}{1} = 6.0000\) mol
    • \(c\) (Oxygen) \(= \dfrac{43}{16} = 2.6875\) mol
    • \(d\) (Nitrogen) \(= \dfrac{0.8}{14} = 0.0571\) mol
  3. Methane yield (\(m\)) per 100 g of dry material:\[m = \dfrac{4(3.6667) + 6.0000 - 2(2.6875) - 3(0.0571)}{8} \]\[m = \dfrac{14.6668 + 6.0000 - 5.3750 - 0.1713}{8} = \dfrac{15.1205}{8} = 1.890\text{ mol of }CH_4 \]
  4. Scale to total mass (455 g):
    • Mass of \(CH_4\) per 100 g dry \(= 1.890 \times 16 = 30.24\) g
    • Total \(CH_4\) from 1 kg MSW \(= 30.24 \times \dfrac{455}{100} = 137.59\) g

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 137.6 g | Accepted key range: 135.0 to 140.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2019 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: Consider the reactor shown in the figure. The flow rate through the reactor is Q m³/h. The concentrations (in mg/L) of a compound in the influent and effluent are C₀ and C, respectively. The compound is degraded in the reactor following the first order reaction. The mixing condition of the reactor can be varied such that the reactor becomes either a completely mixed flow reactor (CMFR) or a plug-flow reactor (PFR). The length of the reactor can be adjusted in these two mixing conditions to L_CMFR and L_PFR while keeping the cross-section of the reactor constant. Assuming steady state and for C/C₀ = 0.8, the value of L_CMFR/L_PFR (round off to 2 decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment Kinetics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Constant reactor cross-section: \(A\)
    • First order decay reaction constant: \(k\)
    • Removal efficiency target: \(C/C_0 = 0.8\)
  • Aim: Evaluate the ratio \(L_{CMFR} / L_{PFR}\) for the required lengths of Completely Mixed Flow Reactor (CMFR) and Plug-Flow Reactor (PFR).

3. Core Concepts:

CMFR Performance Equation: Based on a single mixed macroscopic mass balance:

\[V_{CMFR} = \dfrac{Q}{k} \left(\dfrac{C_0}{C} - 1\right) \]

PFR Performance Equation: Follows integrated differential mass balance, identical functionally to batch reactors:

\[V_{PFR} = \dfrac{Q}{k} \ln\left(\dfrac{C_0}{C}\right) \]

For constant flow \(Q\) and equal cross-sectional areas (\(V = A \times L\)), the lengths scale proportionally to respective volumetric requirements.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Isolate the \(C_0/C\) term from the target remaining concentration factor.
  2. Construct parametric equations for both \(L_{CMFR}\) and \(L_{PFR}\).
  3. Divide the expressions to get a clean ratio that cancels out \(Q\), \(A\), and \(k\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the required inverse reduction factor:\[\dfrac{C}{C_0} = 0.8 \implies \dfrac{C_0}{C} = \dfrac{1}{0.8} = 1.25 \]
  2. Formulate reactor length expressions using \(L = V/A\):
    • For CMFR:\[L_{CMFR} = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \left(\dfrac{C_0}{C} - 1\right) = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k}(1.25 - 1) = \dfrac{0.25\,Q}{A \cdot k} \]
    • For PFR:\[L_{PFR} = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \ln\left(\dfrac{C_0}{C}\right) = \dfrac{Q}{A \cdot k} \ln(1.25) \approx \dfrac{0.22314\,Q}{A \cdot k} \]
  3. Calculate ratio \(L_{CMFR}/L_{PFR}\):\[\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{0.25}{\ln(1.25)} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.22314} = 1.1203 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.12 | Accepted key range: 1.10 to 1.15

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: There are 20,000 vehicles operating in a city with an average annual travel of 12,000 km per vehicle. The NOx emission rate is 2.0 g/km per vehicle. The total annual release of NOx will be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Number of Vehicles (\(N\))20,000vehicles
    Average Annual Travel (\(d\))12,000km/year/vehicle
    NOx Emission Rate (\(E\))2.0g/km/vehicle
  • Aim: Calculate total annual NOx release in kg.

3. Core Concepts:

Emission Inventory Formula:

\[M = N \times d \times E \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate total distance traveled by all vehicles.
  2. Multiply by emission rate to get total mass in grams.
  3. Convert grams to kilograms.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Total Distance\[\text{Total Distance} = 20{,}000 \times 12{,}000 = 24 \times 10^7 \text{ km} \]
  2. Step 2: Total NOx in grams\[M_{\text{g}} = 24 \times 10^7 \times 2.0 = 48 \times 10^7 \text{ g} \]
  3. Step 3: Convert to kg\[M_{\text{kg}} = \dfrac{48 \times 10^7}{1000} = 480{,}000 \text{ kg} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4,80,000 kg | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A city generates \( 40 \times 10^6 \) kg of municipal solid waste (MSW) per year, out of which only 10% is recovered/recycled and the rest goes to landfill. The landfill has a single lift of 3 m height and is compacted to a density of 550 kg/m³. If 80% of the landfill is assumed to be MSW, the landfill area (in m², up to one decimal place) required would be _______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Landfill Design & Waste Management

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Annual MSW generation: \(40 \times 10^6 \text{ kg}\)
    Recovery rate: 10% → Landfill fraction: 90%
    Landfill lift height \(H = 3 \text{ m}\)
    Compacted landfill density \(\rho_{\text{landfill}} = 550 \text{ kg/m}^3\)
    MSW occupies 80% of total landfill volume
  • Aim: Calculate required landfill area (m²)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Mass-volume-density relationship: \(V = M/\rho\)
  • Volume allocation: MSW volume is fraction of total landfill volume
  • Area calculation: \(A = V_{\text{total}}/H\)
  • Standard practice: Account for cover material, gas vents, liner systems in volume allocation

4. Solution Method:

  • Calculate mass of MSW to landfill
  • Convert to compacted MSW volume
  • Account for 80% MSW occupancy to find total landfill volume
  • Divide by lift height for area
  • Unit discipline: kg → m³ via density; ensure consistent SI units throughout

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate MSW mass to landfill:
    \[M_{\text{landfill}} = 40 \times 10^6 \text{ kg} \times (1 - 0.10) = 36 \times 10^6 \text{ kg} \]
  2. Calculate volume of compacted MSW:
    \[V_{\text{MSW}} = \dfrac{M_{\text{landfill}}}{\rho_{\text{landfill}}} = \dfrac{36 \times 10^6 \text{ kg}}{550 \text{ kg/m}^3} = 65454.545 \text{ m}^3 \]
  3. Account for 80% MSW occupancy (20% for cover, etc.):
    \[V_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{MSW}}}{0.80} = \dfrac{65454.545}{0.80} = 81818.182 \text{ m}^3 \]
  4. Calculate required area for 3 m lift height:
    \[A = \dfrac{V_{\text{total}}}{H} = \dfrac{81818.182 \text{ m}^3}{3 \text{ m}} = 27272.727 \text{ m}^2 \]
  5. Round to one decimal place:
    \[A \approx 27272.7 \text{ m}^2 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer(for NAT): \(27272.7\) m² | Accepted range: 27271 to 27274

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A rapid sand filter comprising a number of filter beds is required to produce 99 MLD of potable water. Consider water loss during backwashing as 5%, rate of filtration as 6.0 m/h and length to width ratio of filter bed as 1.35. The width of each filter bed is to be kept equal to 5.2 m. One additional filter bed is to be provided to take care of break-down, repair and maintenance. The total number of filter beds required will be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Net filtered output required: \(99 \text{ MLD}\)
    • Water loss during backwashing: \(5\%\)
    • Rate of filtration: \(V_f = 6.0 \text{ m/h}\)
    • Width of filter bed: \(B = 5.2 \text{ m}\)
    • Length/Width ratio: \(L/B = 1.35\)
    • Standby units: 1 (for breakdown/maintenance)
  • Aim: Find the total number of filter beds required.

2. Core Concepts:

Total Flow Calculation: Because 5% of the gross filtered water is lost in backwashing, the 99 MLD output represents 95% of the total water filtered.

\[Q_{gross} = \dfrac{Q_{net}}{1 - \text{loss fraction}} \]

Required Area: \(\text{Total Area} = \dfrac{Q_{gross}}{V_f}\)

Number of operational units: \(N_{op} = \dfrac{\text{Total Area required}}{\text{Area of one bed}}\)

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Determine Gross Filtered Water Requirement\[Q_{gross} = \dfrac{99}{0.95} = 104.21 \text{ MLD} \]Convert to \(\text{m}^3/\text{h}\):\[Q_{gross} = \dfrac{104.21 \times 10^6}{1000 \times 24} = 4342.105 \text{ m}^3/\text{h} \]
  2. Step 2: Calculate Surface Area of One Filter Bed\[L = 1.35 \times B = 1.35 \times 5.2 = 7.02 \text{ m} \]\[\text{Area}_{bed} = 7.02 \times 5.2 = 36.504 \text{ m}^2 \]
  3. Step 3: Discharge Capacity of One Filter Bed\[Q_{bed} = 36.504 \times 6.0 = 219.024 \text{ m}^3/\text{h} \]
  4. Step 4: Number of Filter Beds\[N_{op} = \dfrac{4342.105}{219.024} = 19.82 \approx 20 \text{ (rounded up)} \]\[\text{Total Beds} = N_{op} + 1\text{ (Standby)} = 20 + 1 = 21 \text{ beds} \]

    Note: GATE accepted both 21 and 22. Some designers assume an additional bed is concurrently taken offline for routine backwashing alongside the general standby unit. By standard normative calculations, 21 is mathematically rigorous.

4. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 21 | Correct option: (C) (GATE Key: C or D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A water sample analysis data is given below.

IonConcentration, mg/LAtomic Weight
Ca²⁺6040
Mg²⁺3024.31
HCO₃⁻40061


The carbonate hardness (expressed as mg/L of CaCO₃, up to one decimal place) for the water sample is _______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) = 60 mg/L, Atomic Weight = 40
    • \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) = 30 mg/L, Atomic Weight = 24.31
    • \(\text{HCO}_3^-\) = 400 mg/L, Molecular Weight = 61
  • Aim: Calculate Carbonate Hardness (CH) in mg/L as \(\text{CaCO}_3\), to one decimal place.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Total Hardness (TH): Sum of multivalent cations converted to equivalent \(\text{CaCO}_3\).
  • Total Alkalinity (TA): Anions causing alkalinity converted to equivalent \(\text{CaCO}_3\).
  • Carbonate Hardness: \(\text{CH} = \min(\text{TH},\ \text{TA})\)
  • Equivalent Weight: \(\text{Eq. Wt.} = \dfrac{\text{Molecular Weight}}{\text{Valency}}\)
    • \(\text{CaCO}_3\): Eq. Wt. \(= 100/2 = 50\)
    • \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\): Eq. Wt. \(= 40/2 = 20\)
    • \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\): Eq. Wt. \(= 24.31/2 = 12.155\)
    • \(\text{HCO}_3^-\): Eq. Wt. \(= 61/1 = 61\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert all concentrations to mg/L as \(\text{CaCO}_3\).
  2. Apply \(\text{CH} = \min(\text{TH}, \text{TA})\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Total Hardness (TH)\[\text{TH} = 60 \times \dfrac{50}{20} + 30 \times \dfrac{50}{12.155} \]\[\text{TH} = 60 \times 2.5 + 30 \times 4.1135 = 150 + 123.405 = 273.405 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3 \]
  2. Step 2: Total Alkalinity (TA)\[\text{TA} = 400 \times \dfrac{50}{61} = 400 \times 0.81967 = 327.868 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3 \]
  3. Step 3: Carbonate Hardness
    Since \(\text{TH} (273.405) < \text{TA} (327.868)\):\[\text{CH} = \text{TH} = 273.4 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 273.4 mg/L | Accepted key range: 272.0 to 274.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The ultimate BOD (\( L_0 \)) of a wastewater sample is estimated as 87% of COD. The COD of this wastewater is 300 mg/L. Considering first order BOD reaction rate constant k (use natural log) = 0.23 per day and temperature coefficient θ = 1.047, the BOD value (in mg/L, up to one decimal place) after three days of incubation at 27°C for this wastewater will be _______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Ultimate BOD: \(L_0 = 87\%\) of COD
    • COD = 300 mg/L
    • BOD rate constant at 20°C: \(k_{20} = 0.23 \text{ day}^{-1}\) (base \(e\))
    • Temperature coefficient: \(\theta = 1.047\)
    • Incubation time: \(t = 3\) days at \(T = 27^\circ\text{C}\)
  • Aim: Calculate BOD exerted (\(y_t\)) in mg/L after 3 days at 27°C.

3. Core Concepts:

BOD Kinetics:

\[y_t = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) \]

Temperature Correction (Arrhenius):

\[k_T = k_{20} \cdot \theta^{(T-20)} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine \(L_0\).
  2. Adjust \(k\) from 20°C to 27°C using \(\theta\).
  3. Calculate the 3-day BOD using \(k_{27}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Ultimate BOD\[L_0 = 0.87 \times 300 = 261 \text{ mg/L} \]
  2. Step 2: Temperature-Corrected Rate Constant\[k_{27} = 0.23 \times (1.047)^{(27-20)} = 0.23 \times (1.047)^7 = 0.23 \times 1.3796 = 0.31731 \text{ day}^{-1} \]
  3. Step 3: BOD at 3 Days\[y_3 = 261 \times (1 - e^{-0.31731 \times 3}) = 261 \times (1 - e^{-0.95193}) \]\[y_3 = 261 \times (1 - 0.3860) = 261 \times 0.6140 = 160.25 \text{ mg/L} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 160.2 mg/L | Accepted key range: 154.0 to 161.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A waste activated sludge (WAS) is to be blended with green waste (GW). The carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) contents, per kg of WAS and GW, on dry basis are given in the table.

ParameterWASGW
Carbon (g)54360
Nitrogen (g)106


The ratio of WAS to GW required (up to two decimal places) to achieve a blended C:N ratio of 20:1 on dry basis is _______
questions.explanation:
Solid Waste Management | Composting

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ComponentCarbon (g/kg)Nitrogen (g/kg)
    Waste Activated Sludge (WAS)5410
    Green Waste (GW)3606
  • Target blended C:N ratio = 20:1
  • Aim: Find the blending mass ratio \(R = M_{WAS} / M_{GW}\).

3. Core Concepts:

By conservation of mass, total carbon and nitrogen in the blend are sums from each component:

\[\dfrac{C_{blend}}{N_{blend}} = \dfrac{M_{WAS} \cdot C_{WAS} + M_{GW} \cdot C_{GW}}{M_{WAS} \cdot N_{WAS} + M_{GW} \cdot N_{GW}} \]

Dividing numerator and denominator by \(M_{GW}\) gives a direct equation in \(R\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute \(R = M_{WAS}/M_{GW}\) and set the blend ratio equal to 20.
  2. Solve the resulting linear equation for \(R\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1: Setup Mass Balance\[\dfrac{54R + 360}{10R + 6} = 20 \]
  2. Step 2: Solve for \(R\)\[54R + 360 = 20(10R + 6) \]\[54R + 360 = 200R + 120 \]\[240 = 146R \]\[R = \dfrac{240}{146} = 1.6438 \approx 1.64 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.64 | Accepted key range: 1.60 to 1.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: As per IS 10500:2012, for drinking water in the absence of alternate source of water, the permissible limits for chloride and sulphate, in mg/L, respectively are
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Standards

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: IS 10500:2012 — Indian Standard Drinking Water Specification.
  • Condition: Drinking water in the absence of alternate source (Permissible Limits).
  • Aim: Find the permissible limits for Chloride and Sulphate.

IS 10500:2012 defines two tiers of limits:

  • Acceptable Limit: Up to which water is generally acceptable.
  • Permissible Limit: Acceptable only in the absence of an alternate source.

Option (A): 250 and 200 — Acceptable limits only.

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q15
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
In the figures, Group I represents the atmospheric temperature profiles (P, Q, R and S) and Group II represents dispersion of pollutants from a smoke stack (1, 2, 3 and 4). In the figures of Group I, the dashed line represents the dry adiabatic lapse rate, whereas the horizontal axis represents temperature and the vertical axis represents the altitude.

The correct match is
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution and Dispersion

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Group I (Temperature profiles): Superadiabatic (P), Adiabatic (Q), Inversion (R), Inversion over superadiabatic (S)
    • Group II (Plumes): Looping (1), Coning (2), Fanning (3), Fumigation (4)
  • Aim: Correctly match atmospheric temperature profiles to plume shapes.

3. Core Concepts:

ProfileConditionStabilityResulting Plume
P — SuperadiabaticELR > DALRHighly UnstableLooping (1) — wavy, touches ground randomly
Q — AdiabaticELR ≈ DALRNeutralConing (2) — symmetric cone due to mechanical turbulence
